Abu Dhabi National Oil Company vessel damaged in attack, UAE says
A vessel with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) Logistics and Services was damaged in an attack Tuesday afternoon, the United Arab Emirates state-run news agency (WAM) reported.
The attack reportedly occurred in the territorial waters of the UAE and "response efforts" were ongoing, according to WAM.
Iran war 'not necessarily popular,' Hegseth says

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth acknowledged that the ongoing war with Iran is "not necessarily popular" among American voters, when asked about the role the conflict played in the heavy Republican defeat in the midterm elections.

Vice President JD Vance last week publicly blamed the conflict for the historic Democratic Party victory in the midterm elections. Asked about Vance's remarks, Hegseth said he did not want to engage in "finger pointing."
Hegseth said the war was launched "for the right reasons, to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon."
Paraphrasing Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Hegseth said of the war, "It's not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary. And that's certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking."
Hegseth says US can 'maintain oversight' of Iranian nuclear sites

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said during Tuesday's press conference that the U.S. can "maintain oversight" of Iranian nuclear sites and any attempts by Tehran to reconstitute its military capabilities.
"We're able to maintain oversight and visibility of those nuclear sites. And if we saw the kind of nefarious activity that required action, we would take it," Hegseth said.

Hegseth said the ongoing U.S. blockade of Iranian ports is "ironclad," suggesting that operation -- alongside the damage done to Iran's industrial base -- means Tehran's "ability to reconstitute is much less than ours."
"We know that they're going to attempt to reconstitute. We know that we are in a much stronger position," Hegseth said.
Hegseth defends US campaign in Iran, claims 'historic military victory'

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said during a Tuesday morning press conference that the U.S. had achieved "a historic military victory," over Iran, as he faced a House impeachment resolution introduced by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie.
Hegseth defended his tenure as Pentagon chief, including the ongoing U.S.-Israeli campaign against in Iran, which began in February, and last summer's 12-day U.S.-Israeli conflict with Tehran.
"More than 13,000 targets struck. Their navy sunk. Their air force grounded. Their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said, listing military statistics from the conflict to date.

"More than 80% of their nuclear industrial base gone. Their military in ruin. The ironclad blockade unbroken. We control the Strait of Hormuz. Crazy Islamists in Tehran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. A historic effort only made possible by a courageous commander in chief," Hegseth added, referring to President Donald Trump.
"He did not kick the can. He kicked their teeth in," Hegseth said of the president.

"We will not apologize for destroying the capabilities of a regime that chants, 'Death to America," Hegseth continued. "And if that regime makes one wrong move, as the president said, we remain locked and loaded with the full weight and lethality of Central Command."

title: Trump says he'd 'stand by' Hegseth even if he's impeached
summary: Hegseth said he's "not worried" about an impeachment effort.
story: The House must take up the impeachment resolution within two legislative days.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor Monday afternoon.
Massie read aloud all eight articles of impeachment he filed against Hegseth, speaking for about 1 hour and 20 minutes.
He explained his resolution afterward.

"[President Trump and Secretary Hegseth] didn't meet the requirements to take action without Congress," Massie told reporters regarding the Iran war, later adding, "Like there's no argument here. If this were in a courtroom, we wouldn't need witnesses. We wouldn't need to provide evidence."

The House must take up the measure, since impeachment is a privileged matter, within two legislative days -- forcing Republicans to go on the record after suffering major losses in the 2026 midterm elections. Calls to impeach Hegseth have grown as several Republicans have attributed the GOP's sweeping midterm losses to the Iran war.
In an impromptu White House briefing Monday afternoon, Trump said he would "stand by" Hegseth, even if he's impeached.
"He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won. I had great people," Trump told reporters.

It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control until Jan. 3. But Massie told ABC News’ Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl that he's confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass.
Massie needs a simple majority for the impeachment resolution to succeed in the House, meaning that just three Republicans need to vote with all Democrats to prevail.
Massie said he thinks impeachment will only be messier if the matter waits until Democrats are in control of Congress in January.

"Will it work? I hope for his sake it does work, because the Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection," Massie told reporters Monday afternoon, adding that he predicted there would be a "robust trial over in the Senate."

It doesn't appear that any Democrats will vote against the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries came out in support of impeaching Hegseth saying on ABC News' "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes."
GOP leaders could offer a motion to "table" the resolution rather than take a direct vote on the underlying measure. That would also need to pass by a simple majority.
Even if the measure passes in the House, it would still need approval by a two-thirds majority in the GOP-controlled Senate, a lofty threshold that's unlikely to be met.

Hegseth said earlier Monday that he's "not worried about" the efforts to impeach him over his controversial leadership at the Pentagon and role administering the Iran war, announcing a rare press conference on the topic set for Tuesday.
"We’re not worried about that,” Hegseth said when asked by a reporter about Republican support on Capitol Hill amid the impeachment effort led by Massie.

"We're going to do a press conference tomorrow morning at the Pentagon on that very topic. So I'll save my remarks there. I hope you all come loaded for bear with your questions," said Hegseth, who hasn't held a press conference since May.
Massie offered a prebuttal to Hegseth's press conference planned for Tuesday, saying he hopes the Pentagon's chief addresses the articles of impeachment.
“Tell us why you are not guilty of each of these eight articles of impeachment," Massie said.

Massie attempted to introduce articles of impeachment in mid-September only to be thwarted by Speaker Mike Johnson, who canceled the final scheduled day of legislative business before the midterm elections -- staving off a vote at the time.
Massie, a conservative who has gained a reputation as a constitutionalist through his seven terms in the House, lost a primary earlier this summer after President Donald Trump endorsed his opponent.

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer declined to back the Hegseth impeachment effort, but Massie volunteered that "there’s a lot of questions about" Hegseth, including the embattled secretary’s strategy in Iran.

"I will weigh the debate and make a decision," retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon told ABC News' Kyra Phillips on Friday when asked if he will vote to impeach Hegseth. "I do think the secretary has made some bad mistakes."
Trump has maintained that he has "every intention to keep" Hegseth atop the Pentagon.
In a video posted Thursday, Hegseth proclaimed that he will not back down -- doubling down on the Iran war and his cultural agenda at the Pentagon while drawing a parallel to Trump.

"This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.

title: Sen. Duckworth wants VA to identify toxic threats before veterans get sick
summary: Sen. Tammy Duckworth to introduce legislation that would require VA to more quickly assess toxic hazards, expanding access to health care and disability benefits.
story: Her bill would expand access to healthcare and disability benefits.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Illinois, is set to introduce legislation Tuesday that would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to more quickly assess toxic hazards in combat zones, expanding access to health care and disability benefits for troops who develop illnesses linked to their service.

The bill would give the VA 180 days to assess toxic hazards, which can include exposure to intense pollution, radiation or chemicals, in any new combat zones troops serve in and recommend whether those who served there should be presumed to have been exposed and potentially eligible of healthcare and compensation, according to an outline of the bill.
There is currently no clear mechanism for adding new combat zones to the list of more than a dozen countries and territories where troops are already presumed to have faced toxic exposure.
It would also require the department to revisit overseas assignments at least every five years, looking for hazards that may have gone unrecognized.

The proposal would expand on the PACT Act, which opened VA care and benefits to millions of veterans in 2022 after years of pressure by veterans groups and key advocates such as comedian Jon Stewart, who had advocated for similar assistance for sick 9/11 first responders.

Duckworth's bill would also add Iran to the list of covered combat zones as a proactive measure. While no specific toxic threat has been identified, the provision would account for potential exposure to environmental hazards as the conflict continues, including those that could arise from damaged oil facilities, chemical spills or the use of chemical weapons.

"With a new generation of troops being thrown into another war in the Middle East, our nation must learn the lessons from previous conflicts and proactively ensure Iran Veterans don't suffer from those same mistakes," Duckworth said in a statement to ABC News.

The PACT Act marked one of the largest expansions of veterans' health care and disability benefits in U.S. history, with nearly $280 billion in new spending projected over a decade, according to an analysis from the Congressional Budget Office.

The bill dramatically eased the burden on veterans seeking disability benefits by easing the need to prove that certain cancers and respiratory illnesses were directly caused by toxic exposure during military service. Instead, qualifying service can be enough to establish that link.

That included veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan exposed to smoke from burn pits, the makeshift garbage disposal sites where troops burned trash, medical waste, jet fuel and plastics, which the VA has linked to a series of respiratory issues and cancers.

The law also expanded presumptions of Agent Orange exposure for veterans who served in Laos, Cambodia and other countries in Southeast Asia during the Vietnam War era. Other provisions covered radiation exposure among troops who responded to the 1968 crash of a nuclear-armed B-52 near Thule Air Force Base in Greenland.

Previously, veterans faced a daunting evidentiary hurdle of documenting exposure that may have occurred decades earlier and proving it caused an illness that surfaced years after leaving the military, claims were often tangled in legal disputes or stuck in a bureaucratic slog.
By May 2024, the VA had approved 1 million claims for healthcare and disability compensation tied to the PACT Act for veterans, according to agency data.

title: California's Prop 40 'billionaires' tax' measure is rejected, AP projects
summary: The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill."
story: The main group opposing the tax raised $333.1 million ahead of the midterms.
Voters rejected California's so-called "billionaires' tax" ballot initiative, according to a projection from The Associated Press on Monday.
This means that the state will not levy a 5% tax on the wealth of California taxpayers and trusts with assets valued over $1 billion. This measure is known as Proposition 40.

The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill." Yes on 40, the main group backing the measure, had said the tax would generate around $100 billion over five years. The measure would have affected roughly 200 of California's billionaires.
Building a Better California, the main group opposing the tax, raised $333.1 million since the beginning of the year. Most of that money came from billionaires.

Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, is the organization's top donor. He gave $102 million to Building a Better California. Because of Brin, "co-founder" is the occupation that gave the most to the group overall, a total of $105.3 million. Donors who listed their occupation as "Investor/Philanthropist" gave the group $47.7 million. CEOs gave $46.6 million. People who listed their occupation as "chairman" contributed $43 million.

Naturally, many of the major donors reported being based in California. $43.9 million came from donors in San Rafael, California, a city in the San Francisco Bay Area. $40.2 million came from West Hollywood. $34.7 million came from Redwood City, another Bay Area city, and $28.4 million came from San Francisco itself.
The largest share of contributions, however, came from Sergey Brin, in Reno, Nevada.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became its most prominent opponent, arguing that the tax could be dodged by billionaires who could leave the state for another. As ABC News has reported, Newsom has shared a counterproposal: a national billionaire tax focused on loans taken against assets.
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna were huge proponents of the measure, arguing that it could set the stage and be an example for a national wealth tax.
Khanna told ABC News in early October that he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both have openly discussed that they are weighing a presidential bid in 2028.

"He [Newsom] doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors?" Khanna said.
Tech investors pushed back hard on the measure. Vinod Khosla warned that the state's top wealth creators would leave, and Mark Cuban told Khanna he doesn't understand business.

title: Trump says Nvidia CEO told him he 'didn't know' he was involved with alleged spy
summary: Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang a day after Nvidia announced an investigation into its CEO.
story: Nvidia has announced an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump said the head of Nvidia told him in a phone call on Monday that he "didn't know" he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump's comments come a day after the tech giant announced an investigation into Jensen Huang following reporting that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about it.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president told reporters during a press briefing.
"I asked him that question -- 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy,' and I really believe him," Trump continued.
Trump dodged multiple questions about when he was first briefed on the matter. At one point, the president said the FBI is investigating.
"I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said, without elaborating.

Trump's comments came the same day a lawsuit seeking class action status was filed in federal court against Nvidia and Jensen Huang, alleging that the company "made false and misleading statements" regarding the CEO's interactions with Alice Huang. The complaint was filed on behalf of an Nvidia shareholder.
On Sunday, Nvidia said that its board launched an independent investigation "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
The statement added that a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," according to the statement.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement further said.
"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," according to the statement.

The New York Times reported late last month that Huang, who runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer, was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot centered around a woman they identified as Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials determined was funneling information to Beijing and had developed a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
The Chinese government has denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an Nvidia spokesperson told ABC News at the time.
However, Nvidia on Sunday shared with ABC News an internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.

Addressing Nvidia staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say, "my responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.

Following the New York Times report, congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter said, in part. It is not known if Huang will appear before the committee.
"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," an NVIDIA spokesperson told ABC News Sunday.

title: Supreme Court lifts pause on border construction in Big Bend, Texas
summary: The construction will include physical walls, access roads and vehicle barriers, according to Trump administration plans.
story: The construction will include physical walls, access roads and vehicle barriers.
The Supreme Court is paving the way for the Trump administration to resume border construction throughout the Big Bend region in Texas, including inside Big Bend National Park.

The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 Monday that the government “is exceedingly likely to prevail” in its argument that a district court lacked jurisdiction to pause construction when it issued a preliminary injunction in October.
The Trump administration’s plans to build a combination of physical walls, access roads and vehicle barriers in the Big Bend region have sparked bipartisan backlash.

In May, ABC News spoke with Charlie Angell, a resident and landowner in Redford, Texas, who said he received a letter from U.S Customs and Border Protection (CBP) alerting him that the government wanted access to his land for border construction purposes and may want to take ownership of it if he declined to agree.

Angell runs an outdoor expedition company out of his property on the banks of the Rio Grande. According to a map of the administration’s plans, his property would be split in half and he’d be cut off from the river, where he often launches kayaks for his business.
“It's devastating for me. I'm almost 60 in August, so that's almost at the end of my career. And I've faced all my life savings and everything into retiring right where I'm at,” he told ABC News.

The plans for Big Bend National Park initially included a physical wall, but after public outcry, the plans were changed to include only a combination of vehicle barriers, roads and surveillance technology.

In their petition to the Supreme Court, the government reiterated its claims that the Big Bend Sector, the largest along the southern U.S. border, is an area of “high illegal entry.” However, opponents of the administration’s plans have expressed doubt about those claims.
According to CBP statistics, only about 1% of encounters with migrants happen in the sector. The rugged, remote and dangerous terrain has long been thought to be one of its most deterring factors.
Plaintiffs challenging the construction in court argued in part that DHS exceeded its authority when it waived several environmental and conservation laws to expedite the construction.

On Monday, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the Department of Homeland Security secretary has wide discretion to waive certain laws in the interest of border security and ruled that the preliminary injunction prevented the government from “advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.”
The court also appeared swayed in part by the Trump administration’s claim that stalling construction was costing nearly half-a-million dollars a day.

Some residents of the Big Bend region worry that the construction will cut off access to the Rio Grande, destroy the natural habitats and beauty that draw thousands of people to the region, and would decimate their local economies, which reply heavily on tourism.

“The Trump administration and its contractors are hellbent on destroying one of America’s greatest national parks, and the Supreme Court just gave them the green light,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity. “This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal. They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”

title: Trump says he plans 'tremendous numbers' of pardons in 2nd half of term
summary: The president also defended his pardons of Jan. 6 rioters.
story: The president also defended his pardons of Jan. 6 rioters.
President Donald Trump said he expects to issue "tremendous numbers" of pardons before he leaves office, adding that while he has the power to pardon himself, he doesn't expect to do so.
Asked during a "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday, Trump added that pardoning himself is "not unreasonable."

"But more importantly, I don’t want to have good people that are serving this country and doing a great job spending the rest of their life like I had to do for four years defending myself by radical left lunatics, by people that were very nasty and mean," Trump told CBS News' Ross Douthat as part of a wide-ranging interview.
He added that he intends "to issue tremendous numbers of pardons," possibly including pardons for those who "got within a thousand miles of the Oval Office" during his term.

Trump's predecessor, President Joe Biden, issued several pardons in 2025 in the final days of his presidency. Those preemptive pardons included close family members, although they did not include the president himself.

"My family has been subjected to unrelenting attacks and threats, motivated solely by a desire to hurt me -- the worst kind of partisan politics," Biden wrote in a statement at the time. "Unfortunately, I have no reason to believe these attacks will end."
Biden also preemptively pardoned several senior members of his administration, including Dr. Anthony Fauci, retired Gen. Mark Milley and lawmakers who served on the House Jan. 6 Committee.
Trump suggested early during his second term that Biden should have also pardoned himself.

"This guy went around giving everybody pardons. And you know, the funny thing, maybe the sad thing, is he didn’t give himself a pardon," Trump said at the time, without giving specifics on what crimes his predecessor could have committed.
In 2024, the Supreme Court decision in Trump vs. US granted Trump sweeping immunity from prosecution. The decision would apply to all U.S. presidents, including Biden.

As Trump again entered office he issued a sweeping series of pardons for defendants charged in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, commuting the sentences of 14 individuals and offering a “a full, complete and unconditional pardon to all other individuals convicted of offenses related to events that occurred at or near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021."
About 1,500 people were to be pardoned, he said at the time.
The president in the "60 Minutes" interview that aired on Sunday defended his pardons for the rioters, some of whom attacked law enforcement.
"I think it's very unfair. I pardoned the J-6s. I don't think any group’s been treated more unfairly than them, and and to this day when they see me, they cry," Trump said.
Asked if he meant that even about the ones who attacked police, he said: "There was some that got rough, but you know, they were rough to them, too."

title: DOJ leadership shakeup continues as Civil Division chief steps down
summary: The head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, Brett Shumate, has submitted his resignation, becoming the latest DOJ leader to step down following the midterms.
story: Brett Shumate is the latest DOJ leader to resign following the midterms.

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, Brett Shumate, submitted his resignation Monday, becoming the latest in a growing number of Senate-confirmed DOJ leaders to step down in a post-midterms shakeup of the nation's top law enforcement agency.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Shumate's resignation in a social media post that highlighted a series of civil litigation priorities during the first two years of the Trump administration.

"Under his leadership, the Division pursued important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies and delivered key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement," Blanche wrote. "The Division also secured historic settlements to end illegal corporate DEI practices and shuttered dozens of clinics which were providing so-called 'gender affirming care' to minors."

Shumate is the fourth top official to resign since last week's midterm elections, following the departure of Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, South Florida U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quinones and National Security Division head John Eisenberg.
It was not immediately clear of the Trump administration planned to push for permanent replacements for the positions before Republicans lose Senate control in January.

Shumate's division is instrumental in litigating on behalf of the administration and defending its policies from civil lawsuits, but in the past year it has found itself aggressively seeking new recruits after seeing a similar exodus of top attorneys at other divisions across the Justice Department.

title: US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase
summary: U.S. authorities have charged three men with plotting a campaign of nearly 20 attacks targeting Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., along with a British military base, RAF Fairford
story: U.S. authorities have charged three men with plotting a campaign of nearly 20 attacks targeting Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., along with a British military base, RAF Fairford

NEW YORK -- Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government.”

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.

British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.

The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.

Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.
Tucker reported from Washington.

title: Ex-officer convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore to keep Massachusetts woman quiet about sex abuse
summary: A former Massachusetts police detective has been convicted of murdering a pregnant woman to keep her from revealing he had sexually abused her when she was 15
story: A former Massachusetts police detective has been convicted of murdering a pregnant woman to keep her from revealing he had sexually abused her when she was 15
BOSTON -- A former police detective was convicted Tuesday of murdering a pregnant Massachusetts woman, Sandra Birchmore, to keep her from revealing that he had sexually abused her when she was 15.

Matthew Farwell, 40, was found guilty of strangling Birchmore on Feb. 1, 2021 — 12 days after a tipster called the suburban Boston police department where he worked and reported that they’d had an improper relationship. Birchmore, who was 23 when she died, had been in a tumultuous relationship with the detective, whom she first met while participating in a Stoughton Police Department youth program as a child.

Prosecutors said Farwell staged the crime scene to make her death look like a suicide — and that it nearly worked. Massachusetts State Police investigators quickly concluded that Birchmore killed herself. But the FBI began looking into the case two years later and concluded it was a homicide.
Federal prosecutors harshly criticized the initial police investigation at Farwell’s trial, saying officers didn’t follow leads and closed the case too quickly.

Farwell’s lawyers acknowledged that the married detective had an affair with Birchmore, but said it began when she was 16, making her old enough to consent under Massachusetts law. They also maintained that he did not kill her. They argued that Birchmore had threatened suicide before and that she killed herself after he went to her apartment to break up with her.
Farwell’s conviction carries a mandatory life sentence.
The nearly monthlong trial — with about 50 witnesses and 500 exhibits — unfolded in federal court in Boston, partly because local prosecutors never brought criminal charges.

Massachusetts State Police officers and investigators, some with personal connections to Farwell, quickly concluded Birchmore’s death was a suicide after she was found slumped on her apartment floor with a strap around her neck. One investigator, Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Fogarty told jurors, saw nothing suspicious in Birchmore’s apartment and concluded this was a “troubled girl who killed herself.”
The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, initially ruled Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official manner of death to “undetermined.”

The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department who had led an internal affairs investigation into Farwell based on the tip the department received before Birchmore’s death.

Federal investigators concluded the local probe into her death was rushed and compromised. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police looked at Farwell’s phone only after he had deleted texts with Birchmore.

The FBI investigation uncovered about 40,000 texts between Farwell and Birchmore, including some in which they reminisced about having sex when he was 27 and she was 15 — too young to consent under Massachusetts law.
The texts also showed how their relationship grew contentious as Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship.

Texts in late 2020, after she was pregnant, showed they argued over what role, if any, Farwell would play in the child’s life. A paternity test after Birchmore’s death revealed a different man was the father.
At trial, a digital forensics expert testified that Birchmore’s phone stopped moving three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving her building on the night of her death.
An expert hired by prosecutors, Dr. William Smock, testified that Birchmore’s injuries indicated she was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying.
A defense expert, Dr. Thomas Andrew, the former chief medical examiner in New Hampshire, dismissed Smock’s determination that it was a homicide.

title: NYC sightseeing helicopter makes emergency landing after reporting possible engine trouble
summary: A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight has made an emergency landing at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble
story: A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight has made an emergency landing at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble
BAYONNE, N.J. -- A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.

Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.

In a recording of the air traffic control audio posted on the ATC app, the pilot can be heard saying, “Mayday, mayday, mayday" and “We need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.

Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.

Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards."
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

title: The US to become first nation to fully shun a UN Human Rights Council review
summary: The United States is to become the first country to skip a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s Human Rights Council
story: The United States is to become the first country to skip a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s Human Rights Council
GENEVA -- The United States is set Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.

Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind.
It did not.
“(W)e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the spokesperson said, alleging the council's “persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators.”
The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations — which at times can include a dozen officials or more — make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.
Critics of the U.S. snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries — many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors — to follow suit.

Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: “The administration is saying to the world, ‘we don’t care about whether you would review us or not, we’re going to continue to violate human rights unabashed’."

"And we are saying: ‘No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable’,” he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the U.S. rights record.
He said the ACLU and allies have called on the U.N. human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.
Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system.
“If the predominant global power — which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms — doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.

title: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35%
summary: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35%
story: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35%
HONG KONG -- China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports in October surged 35%.

title: Faced with influx, prosecutor in Washington says he lacks resources to defend immigration cases
summary: The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington says it no longer has the staffing to defend every habeas corpus case and will let judges rule without government opposition
story: The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington says it no longer has the staffing to defend every habeas corpus case and will let judges rule without government opposition

TACOMA, Wash. -- Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they're being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the staffing to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition.

Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors' resources.

“Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents," Floyd wrote.

The backlog has “severely impacted the government's ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn't specify how many cases could be affected.

Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda.
Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.
The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

title: Court clears the way for border wall construction in Texas’s Big Bend to resume
summary: The Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas
story: The Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas

WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.
The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of border barriers a week across the entire border.

The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.
In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.

They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.

A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.

The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.

The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting.

title: Democrats plan to use new power to rein in Trump's education agenda, but their tools are limited
summary: Democrats in Congress are gearing up to challenge President Donald Trump's education policies, including the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department
story: Democrats in Congress are gearing up to challenge President Donald Trump's education policies, including the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department

WASHINGTON -- Democrats in Congress are preparing to flex their soon-to-be majorities in opposition to some of President Donald Trump’s marquee education policies, starting with the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department. But with Trump threatening to use his veto power, they may be limited to opening investigations and using federal funding as leverage.

The White House has given no sign of backing away from its campaigns to close the department and to end diversity, equity and inclusion policies. But Democrats are preparing to use their oversight and appropriations powers to push back against Trump administration decisions that have reverberated through schools and universities.

Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, said he plans to “leave no rock unturned” as he takes the helm of the panel's investigative powers, which include authority to issue subpoenas and hold hearings.

The committee is preparing to explore the Trump administration's dismantling of the Education Department, its oversight of federal student loans and its anti-discrimination policies, Scott said. Under Trump, the Education Department has prioritized investigations into transgender issues while backing away from addressing systemic racism in schools.
A day after the midterm elections, Scott sent a letter to 10 federal agencies reminding them to preserve records that might become part of a congressional review.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, called on Democrats to “hold the Trump administration accountable for dismantling the Department of Education and turning its back on students.”

Trump officials denounced Democrats' plans, with Education Department spokesperson Savannah Newhouse saying they're plotting to “prematurely sabotage" Education Secretary Linda McMahon. White House spokesperson Liz Huston accused Democrats of failing American students with “disastrous leadership" before Trump returned to office.

Congressional investigations can be used to apply political pressure and uncover how decisions were made, but they are unlikely to present a substantial brake on Trump's education policies that have outraged Democrats over the last two years. And with Trump pledging to veto Democratic bills he sees as harmful, there's little optimism for legislative countermeasures.

“While we’re all very, we’re very happy that this Congress is unlikely to pass legislation like the legislation that was passed last year, it’s not very likely that they will be able to undo the harm that’s already been done,” said Diana Autin, executive director of the SPAN Parent Advocacy Network, a parent-led nonprofit based in Newark, New Jersey.

Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee are exploring harder checks through the budgeting process. Some are planning to add conditions to spending bills aimed at reining in the Trump administration's education agenda.

“I think there will be an interest in using the power of the purse to establish guard rails and prevent these abusive practices,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, told The Associated Press.

Last year, Democrats failed to secure broad language in a funding bill to block further dismantling of the Education Department. Now, with majorities in both chambers, they're preparing to try again. Van Hollen described it as one avenue to “stop the bleeding” but not necessarily to reverse the dismantling that has been done.

“It’s a little harder to try to rebuild an entity just through an appropriations bill,” he said. “But we can certainly try to prevent further damage and then seek to reverse the harm that’s been done.”

There’s also interest in conditioning federal funding to rein in Trump’s battle to reshape higher education, Van Hollen said, including the White House’s repeated efforts to cut funding at Harvard and other prestigious universities. “That said,” he added, “we’re dealing with an administration that has demonstrated no respect for the law.”

Education advocates are pushing Democrats to go a step further. Some hope to see appropriations language ordering the administration to reverse decisions moving Education Department functions to other agencies, including one that put special education programs under the Department of Health and Human Services, and another that put the investigation of school discrimination claims under the Justice Department.

“I think it’s going to become more and more apparent that they don’t have the authority just to keep dismantling some of these offices,” said Aaron Ament, president of the advocacy group Student Defense, which is representing plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the dismantling of the Education Department.

Some advocates are hoping the next Congress will be in place in time to approve the nomination of a replacement for Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general who spearheaded the Justice Department's sweeping investigations into elite universities. She announced her resignation last Thursday in the wake of the midterms. Alarming to some education advocates, however, is Trump's decision promoting Stephen Miller, the architect of some of Trump's most hard-line policies, to chief of staff.

Todd Wolfson, president of the American Association of University Professors, said that the higher education environment was so tough that the organization endorsed candidates for the first time during the midterms. Those candidates included Abdul El-Sayed, a former professor, who won a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat. Now, Wolfson is looking not just at reversing some of what has happened during the Trump administration, but building a campaign for a free public higher education system.
“Most other countries have figured this out, and we can too,” Wolfson said.
But with Trump's veto power, such a change is unlikely in the next two years.

Trump’s second term in office has been marked by seismic change in education policy. Trump officials cut the Education Department’s staff by nearly half and signed intergovernmental agreements parceling its top duties to other agencies. In higher education, the administration has mounted a battle to eliminate DEI practices and curb international enrollment, using federal funding as leverage to advance policies favored by the White House.

Yet education issues receded to the background in midterm elections that became a referendum on Trump's deeply unpopular economic policies and the Iran war. As Democrats sort out a vast oversight agenda, education is expected to fall farther down the list of priorities, behind big topics like Trump's self-enrichment and federal immigration raids.
Despite their new power, there's little optimism that Democrats will be able to override Trump's veto on big education bills. Some advocates want lawmakers to try anyway.
“Even if he vetoes them, let’s put the pressure on to get it to his desk, and then you see what the contrast is,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers union.

Some on the right are pushing for last-minute legislation to advance Trump's agenda. A day after the midterms, the Heritage Foundation asked Republican lawmakers to propose a bill to close the Education Department and strip any mention of it from federal law. In what amounts to a political Hail Mary, the group argued the agency has failed to prove its value since it opened in 1980.
The letter asked Republicans to collaborate with McMahon “to sunset this failed bureaucracy.”
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kansas.

title: Karen Attiah won't rejoin Washington Post after being fired for Charlie Kirk comments
summary: Former Washington Post opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her old job
story: Former Washington Post opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her old job

WASHINGTON -- Opinion writer Karen Attiah has decided not to return to her job at The Washington Post, despite winning reinstatement after her firing over social media posts about the 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
Attiah wrote Sunday on her Substack, “The Golden Hour by Karen Attiah,” that she reached a settlement with the Post and plans to move forward with her life and career.

“While I remain proud of the victory, I came to the painful realization that returning to The Washington Post meant coming back without the guaranteed freedom and institutional support to do what I loved: use my voice, seek truth, and serve readers,” Attiah wrote.
Attiah didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. A Washington Post spokesperson declined to comment Monday on Attiah's decision.
At the time of her firing, Attiah was the only Black full-time member of the Post’s opinion desk.
In August, an arbitrator ordered the newspaper to reinstate Attiah, ruling that it didn't have sufficient cause to fire her and ordering it to award her full back pay and lost benefits.

Kirk, who was white, launched the conservative Turning Point USA in 2012 and made provocative statements about race, gender and politics. He was critical of the Black Lives Matter movement on college campuses and called George Floyd, the Black man whose 2020 murder at the hands of Minneapolis police sparked protests, a “scumbag.”

Kirk, 31, also was an ally of President Donald Trump and used his popular podcast to espouse rhetoric many critics felt was racist and divisive. He was shot and killed Sept. 10, 2025, during an event at Utah Valley University.
His death elicited a torrent of comments from Trump and others about him, both pro and con.

After Kirk’s killing, Attiah made several social media posts, including “if anything, the rush to coddle violent white men is self-protective — that we know they are not used to feeling vulnerable and mortal — and will react violently out of fear. And we will all suffer.”
The Post fired Attiah in an email, accusing her of “gross misconduct.”

“Your public comments on social media regarding the death of Charlie Kirk violate the Post’s social media policies, harm the integrity of our organization, and potentially endanger the physical safety of our staff,” it wrote.

Attiah was among dozens of people from various professions who were fired over comments they made about Kirk’s assassination, which raised questions over free speech as Trump vowed retribution for remarks he considered disparaging.

The Democracy Defenders Fund and the Washington-Baltimore News Guild, which represented Attiah, didn't immediately respond to Monday messages seeking comment about Attiah's decision not to return to the paper. At the time of the arbitrator's ruling, they said the ruling marked a landmark moment for press freedom.

title: Senate advances sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
summary: The Senate is moving forward with bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for data centers and infrastructure projects
story: The Senate is moving forward with bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting for data centers and infrastructure projects

WASHINGTON -- The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to power data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.
While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.
The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: “Well, the bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump’s opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration’s efforts to block Maryland’s pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.
Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America,'' adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.
But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.
McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

title: School closures are accelerating in US, but more financial pain lies ahead
summary: Students in Vallejo, California, faced a challenging start to the school year as they adjusted to a new school after their previous one closed
story: Students in Vallejo, California, faced a challenging start to the school year as they adjusted to a new school after their previous one closed
VALLEJO, Calif. -- Minutes before first bell, Penny Núñez-Brandão scanned the crowd outside Glen Cove Elementary School, looking for familiar faces.
“I don’t see any,” the fifth grader told her mom one morning in August. “None of my friends are coming.”

The start of a new school year can be nerve-wracking under any circumstances. But for Penny and thousands of students across the U.S., this academic year brought the added difficulty of adjusting to an entirely new school after their previous ones shuttered. As U.S. birth rates continue a multidecade slide and state and federal education funding dries up, an increasing number of cash-strapped school districts around the country have resorted to closing campuses to save money.

A total of 1,156 schools closed during the last academic year — the highest number since the pandemic, according to an analysis of federal data by Big Local News at Stanford University. At the same time, new research shows student enrollment has fallen much faster than schools are closing, suggesting more painful financial choices lie ahead.
AP is covering school closures in partnership with The Hechinger Report and Big Local News at Stanford University.

The Vallejo City Unified School District, a working-class district near San Francisco, serves half as many students as it did two decades earlier. District leaders have closed five campuses since 2025 — a quarter of its schools. They’ve also placed up to a third of all staff positions on the chopping block to help plug a staggering $36 million deficit.

Still, research shows closing schools rarely yields the financial relief districts hope for. Busing students to their reassigned schools, severance for pink-slipped staff and security for empty facilities often eat up any savings. School closures can also set students back academically and make it harder to attract teachers, who may worry the jobs aren’t stable.

Closing schools can also trigger a downward spiral, as frustrated families flee to charter or private schools or other districts. In Vallejo, some parents said they chose to homeschool this fall or were planning to sell their homes and move to neighboring districts.

“Families are literally packing up their kids and moving away,” said Penny’s mother, Kimberly Núñez-Brandão, who already moved her older son to a competing charter school. She recently attended Glen Cove’s curriculum night for families and shared her shock at learning Penny’s new teacher had 32 students in his first class.
“They already overwhelmed teachers with 30-plus students,” she said. “Who’s winning here?”

Rubén Aurelio, superintendent for Vallejo schools, acknowledged cuts and closures can be hard for families but said they are necessary to correct for school districts and budgets designed for a different reality.

“We’re not just closing schools to close schools,” Aurelio said. “We’re right-sizing a district that was built for significantly more kids. And if we’re going to actually improve outcomes for the kids we still have, we need to concentrate resources.”

Nationwide, public school enrollment fell by more than 1.4 million students, roughly 3%, between fall 2019 and 2024, according to an Associated Press analysis of federal education data collected by Stanford University economist Thomas Dee and sociologist Jaymes Pyne. The total number of schools has declined, too — but only to about pre-pandemic levels, the researchers found, suggesting closures are lagging enrollment declines.

Lower birth rates are the primary reason for enrollment decline, but a federal crackdown on immigration and the post-pandemic expansion of private school vouchers and homeschool options have contributed to the decline. Bellwether and WestEd, two research groups, recently estimated declining enrollment could cause schools to lose $11.5 billion in state revenue annually by 2030-2031, potentially prompting widespread layoffs, cuts to academic programs and school closures.

In Vallejo, a city still struggling to bounce back from the closure of a naval base in the 1990s, enrollment has tumbled from nearly 18,000 in the fall of 2006 to about 9,300, according to the district. California has recorded one of the nation’s most precipitous enrollment drops. But school districts throughout the country, including large systems in Cleveland, Houston and Philadelphia, are facing similar closures.
The enrollment and financial situation is unlikely to improve, said Lydia Rainey, research principal at the Center on Reinventing Public Education.
“That’s extremely wishful thinking,” she said. “States aren’t about to open the coffers and swoop in with additional funds to save schools.”
The Vallejo school district is no stranger to budget crises.

In the early 2000s, mismanagement brought Vallejo to the brink of bankruptcy. The state stepped in with a $60 million emergency bailout, which saved Vallejo’s schools from complete financial collapse but kept the district under state oversight until summer 2024. Around the time the state lifted the financial receivership, Aurelio took the helm as superintendent and soon recognized a new set of budget problems.

The district paid for staff salaries using COVID-19 relief money, one-time funding that evaporated early last year. Meanwhile, enrollment dipped below 10,000 students for the first time and was projected to fall further. Vallejo schools, on average, were only 46% full, the district says. Rising inflation and contractual pay hikes further strained the budget.
Aurelio and his team wasted no time in sharing the bad news with families. “I don’t think I ever said, ‘If we close schools.’ I started by saying, ‘When we close,’” he recalled.

In early 2025, the superintendent announced two rounds of closures: The first shuttered two K-8 schools at the end of that academic year. The school board also cut payroll and relocated a district-sponsored charter school to a vacated campus.
Aurelio also set a December 2025 deadline for the board to select three neighborhood schools to close in the second round and approve additional staff cuts.
The tumult has left families wondering about their future in the district.

Caitlin Jackson and her husband, a facilities manager, moved to Vallejo with their toddler son, John, for the relatively affordable homes. But large class sizes and safety concerns dissuaded the new parents from enrolling John in a neighborhood school.
They’re taking a chance on the district-sponsored charter — for now.
“Trying to downsize a system while also trying to sustain it, that is just very difficult,” said Jackson. She said she hasn’t ruled out private school or homeschooling.

The sentiment reflects a real risk for districts that choose to close schools. The already painful cost-cutting measure may push even more families into competing charter networks, neighboring districts or private alternatives — further eroding the funding schools get per enrolled student.

So along with cutting budgets, Vallejo is renovating older campuses, hoping to draw younger parents who can’t afford to start a family in San Francisco. (That new spending has rankled some parents, including Núñez-Brandão.) The superintendent said he also plans to open a Tagalog-language school soon, targeting Filipino families from across the Bay Area.

The district has taken more aggressive steps to preserve its enrollment, too. It’s denied some requests from Vallejo families trying to transfer out. (Permission is required under state law.) It has also tried to preempt families’ departures by adding in-demand classes and offering tours of its remaining schools to showcase academic programs or extracurriculars they might have missed.

Jason Willis, a school finance expert with WestEd who has studied campus closures in the Bay Area, credited Vallejo for spreading the cuts and closures over several years and trying to show parents what Vallejo can offer. He likened the approach to the marketing that charter schools have long used to enroll students.

In its second wave of closures, earlier this year, the district shuttered three of its 10 elementary schools. A facilities committee will eventually decide what to do with the vacant campuses, but for now they are vulnerable to burglaries, forcing the district to spend more on security, said Marin Trujillo Cuevas, the district’s executive director for operations.
Inside the classrooms receiving extra students that first week of school, the logistical strain showed.

Ellen Baker-Valdez, a third grade teacher at Glen Cove, had 34 children assigned to her classroom. She’d jammed desks tightly together, their backpacks and lunch boxes piled in a rolling bin by the door.

Outside another classroom, a mother cornered Aurelio, demanding to know why her son’s disability records hadn’t followed him to his new school. The child’s teacher — a substitute, like 7% of Vallejo’s teachers that first day — struggled to answer her questions and attend to the many crying students in her class.

Marisa de la Torre, a managing director of the UChicago Consortium on School Research, said instability created by school closures may last for a while. Studies from the University of Chicago show that academically, displaced students often suffer long-term drops in reading and math. That’s especially true when students end up at low-performing schools.
“It takes a while to recover, if they recover at all,” she said.
Núñez-Brandão isn’t sure she wants to stick around long enough to find out.

Five years ago, as her son prepared for his fifth grade year at Glen Cove, the district reassigned him along with Penny — then a kindergartner — to Highland Elementary due to scheduling difficulties during the pandemic.
“They’re doing it all over again,” Núñez-Brandão said of her daughter’s experience this year. “And I can promise you: More schools are going to close.”

Weeks into the new school year, Penny still struggled with the transition to Glen Cove. She started to make new friends and said she feels comfortable on campus. She also liked her teacher, a first-year educator who’d joined Vallejo’s teacher residency program, launched last year to attract new educators and improve retention.
But with 32 kids in the class, she said it’s hard to concentrate.

And then, on a Tuesday in October, Núñez-Brandão received a note in the Glen Cove parent portal: Penny’s teacher resigned, effective immediately. The school will rely on a long-term substitute for now, the district said.
That night, Núñez-Brandão decided to call a competing charter school in Vallejo — a campus she and Penny already toured — and ask if they still have room for her daughter.
Cherry Salazar of Big Local News at Stanford University and Sharon Lurye of The Associated Press contributed reporting.
