title: NASA is recruiting new astronauts. Here are the qualifications.
summary: The space agency is recruiting its next class of astronauts as the U.S. plans a new mission to the moon. Here's the kind of person NASA is looking for.
story: NASA is recruiting its next class of astronauts, inviting U.S. citizens to apply before midnight ET on Dec. 3 for the chance to "live and work" on the moon.

The space agency's application portal states there are "few vacancies" for the role, which pays $164,395 annually and requires recruits to relocate to Houston, where they'll work at the Johnson Space Center.

While the job is open to all citizens, applicants must meet certain educational criteria and possess specialized experience. In other words, not just any Tom, Dick or Harriet will qualify for the job.

The next group of astronauts is being selected as the U.S. plans to build a moon base and send crewed missions to the lunar surface. NASA's Artemis II mission recently sent a crew of four astronauts around the moon in April, setting a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from our planet.

"The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork and courage."
Here are the qualifications NASA is looking for in an astronaut.
Educational background
NASA's job application portal states that applicants must fit into one of the following four educational profiles:

A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields. A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner. Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.
Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields.
A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.
Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
Specialized experience

Applicants must also select a discipline they best qualify for based on their work experience, with NASA requiring three years of professional experience after completing their degree program or pilot training.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.Physical science: Three years of related work experience.Engineering: Three years of related work experience.Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.
Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.
Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.
Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.
Physical science: Three years of related work experience.
Engineering: Three years of related work experience.

Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.
Other requirements
Applicants must also pass a series of clearances, including medical and psychiatric exams; vision that can be corrected to 20/20 in each eye; and a background check and drug screening.

Aspiring astronauts must be able "to perform moderate to arduous physical activities, including heavy lifting, crouching, crawling and exposure to inclement weather" and "be willing to work in dangerous, life-threatening situations and live/work in remote, isolated, small or confined spaces for prolonged periods." Applicants also have to pass a swimming test.
On top of that, applicants must "be willing to deploy to space for 12 months or longer, accepting extreme isolation, austere living conditions and separation from loved ones."

title: Musk says Tesla will return some Cybertruck deposits
summary: Musk said Monday that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production pace.
story: Elon Musk said Monday that Tesla will return Cybertruck deposits to some of its customers as the company prepares to wind down production of the electric pickup truck.
In announcing the decision in a Monday social media post, Musk said that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" Tesla's production rate.
"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," the Tesla CEO wrote.
Musk announced last week that Tesla would stop producing the Cybertruck at its Texas factory by mid-2027 to "make room for increased Cybercab production," referring to the company's robotaxi line.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, who is the senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the "writing was on the wall" given the Cybertruck's high price and low demand. Ending production will free up time for Musk to focus on robotics and robotaxis, he added.
In his Monday post, Musk disputed claims that Tesla was ending production of the Cybertruck because it was unprofitable.
Rather, he said, the "opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."
Tesla launched the Cybertruck in 2019 for a starting price of $69,000.

In an X post Saturday, Musk said Tesla would continue Cybertruck production for another eight to nine months before shifting focus to scaling the Cybercab. "There will never be another vehicle like it," he said of the Cybertruck.

title: Stocks rebound after tech selloff that pushed Nasdaq into correction
summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged up in early trading after a Thursday rout driven by concerns about a potential slowdown in data center construction.
story: Stocks clawed back some of their losses on Friday after a steep selloff the previous day driven by concerns over a potential slowdown in data center construction.

The S&P 500 rose 23 points, or 0.3%, to close at 7,377, failing to erase the sharp losses it suffered Thursday on its worst day since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended up 1.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.5%.

"Tech is rebounding after two days of some of the most aggressive selling in a long time, although the rally is very tentative and tepid, without much aggressive chasing," Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a note to investors midday Friday.

Financial markets soared immediately after the midterm elections earlier this week, but quickly reversed course on Thursday as investors assessed whether sweeping Democratic victories could lead to tighter restrictions on building data centers and weaker spending on artificial intelligence.

Although Democrats will control both the House and Senate when newly elected lawmakers take office in January, President Trump will retain veto authority, which will likely limit the passage of major restrictions on data centers. Opposition is more likely to surface at the state and local level, Wall Street analysts said.
As of Friday, voters had approved more than 40 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across the country, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting.

Tech stocks started to recover on Friday, helping pull the Nasdaq higher after a brutal beating on Thursday that caused the index to shed more than 1,400 points and enter a "correction," or when stocks fall at least 10% from their previous peak.

Chipmaker Nvidia — a bellwether for the AI sector — gained 2.5% in afternoon trading, and semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology rose 3.9%. The so-called hyperscalers — the companies leading the data center buildout — saw modest gains, with Google-owner Alphabet climbing 0.8%, Amazon up 0.9% and Meta gaining 2.1%; Microsoft shed 0.6%.

IREN, a company that delivers data centers, compute and software for AI training, reported stronger-than-expected results for its latest quarter. Its stock jumped 19.2%, and it also announced two new contracts signed since the end of the quarter.
"We own the land, the power and the data centers under all of it, which gives us more ways to fund growth and lets us set its pace," co-CEO Daniel Roberts said.
Outside of AI, markets were mixed, and more S&P 500 stocks fell than rose.
Slowing AI investment?

A key question for Wall Street is whether AI companies will deliver the revenue growth investors are banking on. Anthropic, which filed for an initial public offering last month and is expected to debut on the Nasdaq this month, will serve as a critical test case. While filing highlighted rapid growth, the company has yet to turn a profit.

In a research note on Friday, Vicky Redwood, a chief economic adviser at Capital Economics, said the investment advisory firm expects AI to boost productivity but is "less confident that AI revenues will grow rapidly enough to sustain the current pace of investment."
The firm expects AI capital expenditures to slow next year, a development Redwood said could drag on U.S. economic growth.

The stock market rebound on Friday came after the release of the jobs report, which showed robust payroll gains in October. Employers added 165,000 last month, above economists' expectations, while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%.
The burst in hiring increases the odds that Federal Reserve officials will raise interest rates at their next meeting in December and in 2027, according to Wall Street economists.

"A solid October jobs report leaves the Fed free to focus on inflation. We expect rate increases in December and March, with energy and AI spillovers the main risks to inflation," Oxford Economics said in a report.

title: Data centers are unpopular — and a key motor of economic growth
summary: The political backlash against data centers is intensifying, threatening to choke off a critical source of U.S. investment, according to economists.
story: The shifting political winds surrounding data centers could buffet the entire U.S. economy, reducing investment in artificial intelligence and slowing growth, according to Wall Street analysts.

The historic tide of money pouring into AI, from data centers and frontier models to state-of-the-art chips and networking gear, has boosted business investment and financial markets in recent years. Federal Reserve researchers recently estimated that spending on data centers, power facilities and other AI-related tech equipment accounted for roughly 20% of U.S. gross domestic product over the preceding year.

In 2026, spending by "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — the companies racing to build data centers — is set to double to around $800 billion and is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2027, according to Capital Economics. Although slowing that buildout might well serve the public interest, given the widespread opposition to data centers, crimping that flow of dollars will have knock-on economic effects.

"Our economy is leveraged on this idea that AI will make us rich," economist Allison Schrager with the Manhattan Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, told CBS News. "There are risks to making it slower — it will mean slower growth."
"Detrimental effects"

Economists and investors now expect the Democrats' sweeping midterm election wins to both slow and increase the cost of data center development across the U.S. By contrast, those victories are unlikely to completely turn off the spigot, experts said, noting that political opposition to data centers isn't uniform, ranging from support for moratoriums on construction to more moderate proposals.
As a result, investment in data centers is likely to continue in the near term, both for projects currently underway and for facilities that have received permits.

For companies investing in AI, the bigger issue will be continuing such capital expenditures at the same pace even as the productivity gains and profits AI is expected to deliver remain largely unrealized for now.

"The high-level calculations essential to justify that level of CapEx, if sustained, we are talking $2 trillion in revenue for major AI companies by the early 2030s, which seems very unlikely," Capital Economics chief North America economist Stephen Brown told CBS News. "Our view is that because of that, there is likely to be some slowdown in data center construction. We are not saying it will stop altogether, but the level of investment is likely to ease. And that would have some detrimental effects on the U.S. economy."
Impact on stocks and consumer spending
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi thinks investors are willing to continue pouring money into AI for the next couple of years, but said the long-term prospects are less clear.

"There are a lot of questions about whether that capital will continue to be there to fill that hole and, if not, AI companies will have to raise prices to cover costs. Then you won't see the same kind of investment," he said.

In 2025, investment in AI added roughly 0.3 percentage points to real GDP growth, according to Capital Economics, which expects investment in the sector to boost growth by roughly the same amount this year.

If AI investment were to fall in 2028, "It could turn into an outright drag on GDP," Capital Economics chief economic advisor Vicky Redwood said in a research note on Friday, estimating that a 10% annual drop in AI spending from current levels would knock around 0.1% off GDP growth.

If investment in AI slows, the greatest drag on growth could come from reduced consumption, Brown of Capital Economics told CBS News. Higher-income Americans who invested in AI stocks have seen their wealth grow sharply. With the S&P 500 up almost 100% over the past three years, such investors have driven increased spending.

"A big part of the wealth effect is coming from the strong rise in equity prices, and if data center construction slows, the likely weakness we'll see in the equity market is a sign of things to come," said Brown, who estimates that this "wealth effect" is boosting economic growth this year by roughly 0.5%.

If the S&P 500 were to lose 20% of its value, that boost would turn into a 0.5% drag on GDP growth, Brown said. "That would be a 1% hit to GDP," he said. "We would be talking about a sharp slowdown in GDP growth versus a recession."

title: Musk says Tesla will end Cybertruck production next year
summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the electric car maker will halt production of its Cybertruck next year and prioritize self-driving taxis.
story: Tesla's Cybertruck has reached the end of the road.

Elon Musk announced on X Friday that the electric car maker would wind down production of its stainless-steel pickup truck at its Texas factory by mid-2027. Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, said the move is to "make room for increased Cybercab production," referring to Tesla's self-driving taxi.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co, told CBS News in an email that "the writing was on the wall" for the Cybertruck given the vehicle's high price and subpar demand.
Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday following Musk's announcement.

Tesla first unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019, capturing attention for its boxy design and futuristic look. Tesla touted the car as a rolling fortress that could tow 14,000 pounds and withstand hits from sledgehammers and even firearms. But the vehicle has been beset by quality problems and has faced numerous recalls over issues with its rearview camera, pedals and other components.

It's unclear if production of the Cybertruck will continue at other factories, although it appears unlikely. According to Forbes, Tesla's gigafactory in Texas is the only one that currently manufactures the pickup.
Weak sales
Tesla continues to dominate the electric vehicle sector. But most of the company's sales come from its Model Y and Model 3 vehicles, according to Cox Automotive.

Tesla sold only 20,237 Cybertrucks in 2025, down from 38,965 the previous year, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book. After commercial production of the truck started in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 Cybertrucks. The vehicle initially sold for $60,990.

Cybertrucks also became a flashpoint in the debate over Musk's role in the Trump administration as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency. In a sign of protest, some people vandalized Cybertrucks at Tesla dealerships.
"Musk is focused on robotics and the robotaxi era, which frees up production with the Cybertruck ramp now winding down," Ives said.

Tesla unveiled its Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, in 2024. Production of the vehicle began at the company's Texas plant in April, and service began in Austin in September.

Ives expects Tesla to be acquired by Musk's rocket company, SpaceX, next year, a move that would provide the EV company with access to more compute and capital, he said in a note to investors last week.

title: Exit polls show data centers weren't winners in 2026 elections
summary: Big majorities of 2026 election voters opposed the building of data centers in their community.
story: AI data centers were a major factor for over half of voters in the 2026 midterm elections. While they were not the most crucial issue, voters made their opinions on data centers clear.
Big majorities nationally and in all the Senate battlegrounds opposed having one built in their community, according to CBS News exit polls.

This opposition benefited Democratic candidates — most who opposed data centers backed Democrats. But most self-identified Republicans also expressed their resistance to having a new data center in their area too — even as they predominantly voted for Republican candidates.
Views about data centers are connected to voters' views about AI more broadly.
Those who see AI doing more harm than good (which is most voters) are opposed to data centers in their community. Voters who think AI will help society are more open to having one.
Candidates like Democratic Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, among others, made data centers a central part of their campaigns.
Here are voters' views on data centers in selected states. In each, there was majority opposition to new data centers across urban, suburban and rural areas.

CBS News polling conducted earlier this year found public skepticism about having a data center in their area fueled by perceived negative impacts on the environment and resources. More did, however, think that data centers could be good, rather than bad, for local tax revenue.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.
Results will continue to update as more votes are counted.

title: Data center backlash fuels votes for change, stock market swing
summary: Concern over AI and misgivings about data center construction​ helped drive votes​ for change in the midterms — and fueled volatility on the stock market that experts say is likely to continue.
story: Concern over AI and misgivings about data center construction helped drive votes for change in the midterm election — and have fueled stock market volatility that experts say is likely to continue.
Investors are worried that the political shift in Congress could slow the buildout of data centers that power AI, potentially throttling one of the economy's main growth engines.
Voters on Tuesday passed at least 44 of 47 measures proposed across the country to restrict data centers — from outright bans to temporary moratoriums — with a few still pending.

The election also elevated a number of candidates who made stricter regulation of data centers a key part of their campaigns. They include Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and who has promised to halt the construction of new data centers until more safeguards are in place.

"What has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities and there are no rules to protect Texas," Hinojosa told CNN's Jake Tapper on Thursday. "We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."

Texas, which did not have a measure on its ballot on Tuesday, has become one of the leaders in the data center market — accounting for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity expected to come online by 2030.

The state has 169 operational data centers, with 118 under construction and more than 500 planned for the future. Big tech companies like Meta, Google and Microsoft have announced major data center projects in the state over the last two years.

In Georgia, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that she would sign an executive order to pause new data center construction once she gets into office in January.

"A lot of data centers are being built in Georgia because of the incentives that have been attached to those data centers," she said. "So, of course, we're going to have to take a look at what those agreements entail."
Stock market swings
Stocks rebounded on Friday morning after plunging on Thursday, a drop that put the tech-heavy Nasdaq into correction and wiped out post-election gains.

Joe Maher, a markets economist with Capital Economics, said in a report Thursday that it remains to be seen if the midterm's shock to the stock market turns out to be the catalyst that derails the AI equity boom, but said it "strengthens our sense that the boom is in its final innings."
"That is an obvious headwind for the firms directly involved in that build-out," Maher wrote.

OpenAI is responding to the backlash. On Thursday, the company laid out plans to build more trust with local communities and to work with them on the development of data centers. The company said it would no longer use controversial nondisclosure agreements with public officials and provide residents access to construction plans.

The AI boom has driven the stock market to record highs, so reversals could dent millions of Americans' retirement savings and hurt consumer spending, which accounts for roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic activity.

Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, told investors in a research note, "The spending is enormous, borrowing is climbing, and investors want to know when the returns arrive. Asking is healthy. Dumping an entire sector over it is an overreaction."
He added: "[T]ech had become the most crowded trade on the planet. When everyone owns the same stocks, it takes very little to spark a rush for the exit, and the exit narrows fast."
President Trump said he is "100% in favor" of AI and vowed to work with states that want to "become RICH by having them."
"They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say "NO" to the riches they bring!" the president posted on Truth Social.
Cracks in AI sector

CBS News business analyst Jill Schlesinger told "CBS Mornings" that the post-election gains in the stock market were about Tuesday's results as a whole — while the losses that followed appear to reflect that investors have had time to digest the results of the ballot measures around AI.

"What we are hearing is that people are nervous about AI — they want to limit the building of AI," she said. "That hits not just the AI companies, but the companies that are building those data centers, the companies that are providing the chips for AI and other financing of AI. That brought the entire tech index down, but also it spilled over to other indexes."
She warned that people should expect more volatility in the stock market.

"What we are now seeing is a repudiation of the AI story," Schlesinger said. "What were we promised? This is transformative technology, it is, but it's not profitable yet. All these AI companies are investing in each other. The interconnectedness, the use of borrowed money, that is all coming to a place wherein investors are saying, 'Wait a second. If they aren't profitable yet, they owe all this money, what does that mean about the value of the company in and of itself?'"
Schlesinger said the volatility in the AI industry is already impacting the broader stock market, particularly if companies are forced to sell other stocks to cover some of those losses.

"That's where it could spread," she said. "It's not spreading into the economy yet, but if you are a retirement investor, be clear: taking no action is a wonderful action in and of itself long term. Stick with your game plan."

title: Case pitting "ER" against "The Pitt" can proceed, appeals court says
summary: A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.
story: Los Angeles — A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.

A three-judge panel from California's 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from "The Pitt" production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced "ER." But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle - the star of both shows and a producer on "The Pitt" - as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.
The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.

Crichton, the author of "Jurassic Park" and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for "ER," the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed two years ago, before a single episode of "The Pitt" had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.

Warner Bros. Television and CBS News have the same parent company following last month's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by the parent of CBS News, which was known at the time as Paramount Skydance and is now called Skydance.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved the "The Pitt" is derivative of "ER."

The court agreed with the plaintiff that "both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it."

The opinion also said that both feature "very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy."

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that "WBTV continues to maintain that 'The Pitt' is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal's decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds."
The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have "generic similarities" that would exist in "any dramatic story" that features "overworked doctors and staff."

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle, John Wells, who created "The Pitt" and worked on "ER," and R. Scott Gemmill, a "Pitt" executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.
Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges "The Pitt" is a rebranded version of an unauthorized "ER" reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted "frozen rights" provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs or other productions derived from "ER" without Crichton's consent, or his estate's consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed "ER" reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

title: Stocks crater as midterms spur investor exodus from tech and AI
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq is now in a "correction" as Wall Street weighs the impact of the Democrats' wins on the critical AI sector.
story: The stock market tanked on Thursday amid concerns that a shift in congressional political control following the U.S. midterm elections could slow the construction of data centers that power artificial intelligence services.

Stocks sank across the board, but technology companies with a hand in the AI sector were hit especially hard. The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 1,422 points, or 5.5%, to close at 24,315. The drop means the tech-heavy index is now in a "correction," or down more than 10% from its most recent all-time high, set in October.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 335 points, or 4.4%, to end at 7,354, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,833 points, or 3.4%.

The decline continued on markets in Europe and Asia on Friday but U.S. shares were set to trade mixed. Dow futures were down 0.8% at 51,192.00. S&P 500 futures gained ground, adding almost 0.3% to 7,402.50.

Market watchers think the Democrats' sweeping electoral victories this week could bolster opponents of data centers and slow the rollout of the facilities, which have spurred widespread public opposition. Investors are reacting to the growing "headline" risks around AI, according to Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge.

The rout was violent enough to potentially delay the highly anticipated initial public offering by Anthropic, a bellwether for the entire AI business, Crisafulli told investors in a research note. Before the turmoil in financial markets, the IPO had been expected to take place this month and to raise as much as $100 billion.

The sharp drop also marks a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year. Other indexes also surged after the election results eased uncertainty about who will control Washington.
"Visible cracks"

"Even though the market rallied Wednesday after the midterm elections, there were visible cracks in the AI ecosystem, and they widened on Thursday amid investor concerns about a potentially slower data center buildout with Democrats in charge of Congress," Chris Larkin, a managing director of trading and investing for E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, said in an email.
A slowdown in erecting data centers could deal a major blow to AI companies, which are pouring billions into the buildout and banking on widespread adoption of the technology.

"The trigger for these moves appears to be the concern that the Democrats, both in Congress and at the state level, will seek to regulate the AI industry and restrict data center development," Joe Maher, markets economist with investment adviser Capital Economics, said in a report. "The immediate risk is that restrictions on data center construction slow the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. That is an obvious headwind for the firms directly involved in that buildout, whose prospects depend on continued rapid capex growth.
Investors worry that the enormous investment in AI is creating a stock market bubble, which happens when sky-high valuations become detached from companies' underlying fundamentals.
"Whether the midterms shock turns out to be the catalyst that derails the AI equity boom remains to be seen, but it strengthens our sense that the boom is in its final innings," Maher said.

Chip and other AI-exposed stocks took a particular beating on Thursday. Shares of Nvidia, whose advanced chips are a key component in developing ever more powerful AI models, fell 9.2% a day after dropping 3.2%. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%.

Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform, also continued to flail, with its shares falling 10.5% after dropping nearly 25% on Wednesday. The stock, which now hovers around $4, is at an all-time low since the company publicly listed its shares in March of 2024.

In other financial markets, the initial reaction to the election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6% to $97.11 and recovered much of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.

title: Feds warn of potential cyberattacks on industrial refrigerators
summary: After a wave of attacks in Europe, U.S. officials are warning of "ongoing" cyber threats targeting refrigeration systems used in healthcare, agriculture and other industries.
story: The U.S. government encouraged grocery stores, healthcare facilities and other businesses that use commercial refrigeration to tighten their security measures on Thursday following a series of cyberattacks that remotely changed the temperatures of commercial freezers and fridges across Europe.

Five federal agencies issued a joint notice, warning of "ongoing cyber threat activity" that could target refrigeration systems used across healthcare, agriculture, transportation and other U.S. industries.
Bad actors globally are exploiting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in refrigeration systems that are "unpatched" or connected to the internet, the agencies said.

"If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in a statement, which was issued in conjunction with the FBI, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Agriculture and Department of Transportation.

In a fact sheet, CISA said businesses that rely on industrial refrigeration should take precautions to protect their systems, including changing passwords, disconnecting system devices from the internet and making software updates to address vulnerabilities.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,"  Chris Butera, acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity at CISA, said in a statement.
The agencies did not specify if any refrigeration systems have been targeted in the U.S.
Wave of refrigeration attacks

The warning follows reports of refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases in August. The Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, a U.S. federal law enforcement unit, has launched an investigation into the incidents, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News on Thursday.

Similar incidents have occurred around Europe in recent weeks, with hackers targeting fridges and freezers across numerous grocery chains. Food retailers reported unexpected temperature spikes in their refrigeration systems, causing food to spoil in stores in Luxembourg, Belgium and Sweden.

Officials in France, which has also been hit by grocery store cyberattacks, said on Wednesday that its national emergency blood supply network was targeted by hackers who tried to raise refrigeration temperatures at several blood banks.

Joshua Corman, executive-in-residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology, a security think tank, said he expects more such attacks, warning that refrigeration systems used by medical labs, grocery stores and bulk warehouses in the U.S. could be compromised.
"There's only so many players that do industrial-level refrigeration, and they're likely also just as vulnerable," he told CBS News.

title: Live Updates: GOP picks leaders, Hegseth faces impeachment vote
summary: House and Senate Republicans held internal elections for their leadership teams on Tuesday as they prepare to become the minority in January.
story: What to know about Congress today:

House and Senate Republicans held internal elections for their leadership teams on Tuesday as they prepare to become the minority in January, with lawmakers in each chamber taking different approaches to their upcoming stint in the proverbial wilderness.In the House, hard-line conservative Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise to become minority leader. Jordan is a top ally of President Trump and the current chairman of the House Judiciary Committee who has battled with Democrats for years.Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans retained their top leadership, unanimously electing Sen. John Thune of South Dakota as minority leader. Some GOP senators had called for a delay in the final vote to discuss the results of the midterm elections, but Thune ultimately emerged unscathed.The House is set to vote at 5:30 p.m. ET on whether to move forward with the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war with Iran and other issues. Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky is leading the push. Hegseth decried the effort as a "political spectacle" at a press conference Tuesday morning.

House and Senate Republicans held internal elections for their leadership teams on Tuesday as they prepare to become the minority in January, with lawmakers in each chamber taking different approaches to their upcoming stint in the proverbial wilderness.

In the House, hard-line conservative Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise to become minority leader. Jordan is a top ally of President Trump and the current chairman of the House Judiciary Committee who has battled with Democrats for years.

Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans retained their top leadership, unanimously electing Sen. John Thune of South Dakota as minority leader. Some GOP senators had called for a delay in the final vote to discuss the results of the midterm elections, but Thune ultimately emerged unscathed.

The House is set to vote at 5:30 p.m. ET on whether to move forward with the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war with Iran and other issues. Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky is leading the push. Hegseth decried the effort as a "political spectacle" at a press conference Tuesday morning.

title: House GOP elects Jim Jordan as next leader in major shakeup
summary: Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise for the role of minority leader.
story: Washington — House Republicans voted to elevate Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to lead the party in the next Congress, selecting him over current Majority Leader Steve Scalise following the GOP's crippling losses in last week's midterm elections.

Jordan is a hard-line conservative and close ally of President Trump. His ascension to minority leader represents a significant shakeup for House Republicans, who are looking to rebuild after losing more than 40 House seats.
Tuesday's vote was 106 to 73, sources familiar with the tally told CBS News.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom. And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day," Jordan said in brief remarks after the leadership elections.
House Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping down from leadership and has been noncommittal in recent days about his long-term future in Congress.

Jordan and Scalise both ran for House speaker after Kevin McCarthy's ouster in 2023, leading to weeks of turbulence in the House. But Jordan and Scalise failed to unite the party's various factions. Johnson — who was then a little-known conservative with no leadership experience — pulled off a surprise victory with the conference voting unanimously to make him speaker.
Jordan helped start the conservative House Freedom Caucus and has chaired the House Judiciary Committee since 2023.

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democratic majority," Jordan said in his candidacy letter, arguing that he was "battle-tested."
Scalise, a Louisiana Republican, has held leadership roles since 2014, serving as majority and minority whip before becoming majority leader in 2023.

Scalise was critically injured when a gunman opened fire on a congressional baseball practice in 2017. In 2023, Scalise announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He said several months later that he was in remission after undergoing treatment.
"This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me," Scalise said in his letter to his Republican colleagues announcing his candidacy.

Rounding out the rest of the GOP leadership team is Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip, Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan as conference chair and Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia as chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee.
Emmer and McClain hold the same roles in the majority. Jack will replace Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina as chair of the House GOP's campaign arm. Hudson lost his race for reelection.

title: Mississippi Senate race leans Democratic; Colom holds narrow lead
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi leans toward Democrat Scott Colom, who has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge against incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

As of Tuesday afternoon, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just over 2,600 votes, according to CBS News projections. At one point on the morning after the election, a mere few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.

The state's top election official, Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a post on X Monday that seven more counties of the state's 82 counties still needed to upload their unofficial results, with certified results due from all the counties by Friday. He also said 2,732 absentee mail ballots were still out, and the deadline for election officials to receive them would be Tuesday, Nov. 10.

Hyde-Smith, asked by CBS News' Caitlin Huey-Burns what she could have done differently during the campaign to make it less competitive, responded, "I think we worked very hard and had a very good campaign."

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races in the midterms, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours after election night, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. The state is also processing an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Mail ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: Thune wins reelection as Senate GOP leader after midterms losses
summary: Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after their brutal midterm losses.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader on Tuesday, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after the party's brutal midterm losses, which saw at least seven Senate seats fall to the Democrats.
Senate Republicans backed Thune for another two years as leader by acclamation, or without opposition, after meeting behind closed doors in the Old Senate Chamber for much of the day.

Thune, 65, is a South Dakota Republican who was first elected leader after the 2024 elections. He's been in the Senate since 2005 and took the helm two decades later, after working under Sen. Mitch McConnell as the No. 2 Senate Republican.
Well-liked by his conference, there was little doubt that Thune would remain leader. But a last-minute push by several conservative members to delay the elections added a wrinkle.

GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin led the push to delay the vote after the disastrous midterm results for Republicans. He secured signatures from a handful of his colleagues — Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah — to compel a conference meeting ahead of Tuesday's elections. But the effort to delay any further fell short.
Johnson told reporters that Senate Republicans "just can't continue on business as usual" after a "stunning defeat" at the polls.
"I mean, that kind of defeat demands change," Johnson said, when asked whether new leadership was needed.
But Johnson conceded that there wasn't a clear alternative to Thune. He argued that Senate Republicans at least needed to hear from their leadership team about the strategy moving forward.
After meeting behind closed doors for two hours Tuesday morning, and reconvening later in the afternoon, Johnson told reporters that "this has never been anything against John Thune."
"I think he has been very unfairly attacked by our base," Johnson said.
For his part, Thune appeared sympathetic to the efforts to regroup, and he acknowledged that the decision over whether to delay selecting their leaders would ultimately come down to members.

"I think in the end, I think it's important that for purposes of moving forward, that we get some of these issues settled as soon as possible," Thune told CBS News on Monday. "We'll see what our members think tomorrow."

Thune's reelection as leader comes after he led Senate Republicans as they passed the president's massive tax, border security and defense agenda, swiftly confirmed the president's nominees, and approved a handful of bipartisan priorities over the last two years. At the same time, his tenure was marked by two record-breaking government shutdowns, and a White House that often moved out of step with Republicans in Congress.

Some Republicans were critical of Thune's record, arguing that the GOP agenda wasn't aggressive enough. Conservative frustrations came to a head over the SAVE America Act, a controversial election bill that President Trump repeatedly pushed. Thune made clear that the legislation did not enjoy enough support in the upper chamber to move forward.

Ahead of the election, Thune pushed back on the criticism about the Senate GOP agenda, telling CBS News, "I don't know how you could be more aggressive." And he defended Senate Republicans' record, while acknowledging that there were factors beyond their control.

Senate Republicans had entered the midterm cycle with a map that initially looked favorable, offering few pickup opportunities for Democrats. But GOP candidates across the country were routed as cost of living concerns and the war in Iran took center stage, and expanded the map for Democrats. The Senate GOP lost seats in battleground states like Ohio and North Carolina, along with Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. Two Senate contests — Alaska and Mississippi — remain unresolved, and could yield more victories for Democrats.

Thune, in his first floor speech since the midterms, said, "There is no doubt about it, Tuesday night was a tough election night." He said the election results gave Senate Republicans "an opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do better" and "a clear message that this coming Congress needs to double down on the work that we've been doing on affordability."

title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of a week after the election, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — while one Republican won reelection and CBS News estimated four districts with GOP incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

As of Monday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Monday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of a week after the election, Republicans had won 19 seats, Democrats had won eight and there was one district that CBS News estimated was a toss-up, meaning the GOP won't pick up any additional seats.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Democrats have picked up one other seat, and another race is considered a toss-up.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.
Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: Sanders won't back Schumer as Democratic leader in new Congress
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader in the new Congress, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.
story: Washington — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader when the party takes control of the Senate, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.

Sanders made the announcement at a press conference at the Capitol, saying last week's midterm elections were "about change." Democrats will control at least 54 seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

"It was an election across the country, in red states and blue states, where people were looking around them and saying, 'What is going on in America, when I am struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing, and I'm worried not only that my life economically is going nowhere, everything being equal, my kid in the richest country in the history of the world is going to have the lowest standard of living than I do?' And while all of this is going on, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good," Sanders said.

He added: "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, called for "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."
"We need to have that out in the open to show the American people that a new day has come and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington," he said.

Sanders appeared alongside Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said that "whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then in particular how they're going to communicate differently."
Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

No contender has emerged to challenge Schumer's role atop the Senate Democratic caucus, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has come the closest to throwing his hat in the ring. After initially saying he would not pursue the position, Van Hollen has said this week that he's exploring a potential run.
"What I've said from the very beginning is, we shouldn't have a coronation," he said on Monday. "I'm in listening mode and haven't shut the door."
At an event on Tuesday, Van Hollen said he is "in the process right now of calling my colleagues."
"I'm actively calling my colleagues because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus," he said.
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December.

title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
story: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.

The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.
Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:
Senate Battlegrounds

Democrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.

Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.

Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains close. State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.
Democrats on Defense

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities to flip a House seat, after moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Golden's decision not to run for reelection set the stage for a contest between former GOP Gov. Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap. Even though Dunlap conceded, officials in Maine say the race will proceed to a ranked-choice tabulation because LePage was just shy of the 50% mark. The tabulation will start Nov. 9.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate won a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it will go to a runoff between Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.
GOP-Held Battlegrounds
Several races held by Republicans still don't have projections — including in districts that Democrats are hoping to flip.

Colorado's 4th District: Firebrand Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert is running against Democrat Eileen Laubacher. Boebert switched to the district two years ago, after narrowly winning reelection in a more competitive district in 2022.

Florida's 27th District: It's a battle between two former Miami-area news anchors — GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar and Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. Salazar made waves earlier this year when she warned President Trump's immigration policies could alienate Latino voters.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is locked in a tight battle against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount.
Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.
North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans.

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.
North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.
North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.
South Carolina's 2nd District: Longtime Republican Rep. Joe Wilson is running against Democrat Zyon Khalifa.
Please hold...

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed.
California's 4th District: In the Napa Valley area, longtime Rep. Mike Thompson is running against businessman and fellow Democrat Eric Jones.
California's 7th District: This seat was changed significantly by redistricting. Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui is running against another Democrat, Mai Vang.
California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate this week.

title: Judge denounces DOJ lawsuit over California mail ballots
summary: The Justice Department unsuccessfully attempted to force California election workers to set aside mail ballots returned from up to 20,000 alleged noncitizens.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday condemned a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to force California to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 alleged noncitizens as an attempt to "disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty."

The one-paragraph order from U.S. District Judge David Carter came in response to the Trump administration's move to voluntarily dismiss the suit it filed against California officials and Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, just weeks before the midterm elections.

"This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike," Carter wrote. "The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy."

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit after alleging that there were more than 20,000 people who it believed were not U.S. citizens but were registered to vote in California. It sought a court order forcing election workers to separate mail ballots returned by those it had identified as suspected noncitizens.
The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, after voting in California had begun and after hundreds of thousands of mail ballots had already been returned to election offices.

Carter, appointed by former President Bill Clinton, rejected the Trump administration's effort to require election workers to put aside those ballots and not count them until voters' citizenship could be verified. After failing to secure similar relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and the Supreme Court before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the Justice Department notified Carter on Saturday that it would be dismissing the case.

"In light of the Supreme Court's denial, the United States is evaluating how to best ensure that American votes are protected, including by preventing vote dilution by noncitizens," a Justice Department lawyer wrote in a filing.

The Trump administration said that by the time of the court's next hearing in the case, set for Friday, "California will have already commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones. There is then no way to get the challenged ballots segregated. As a result, the relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary."
In his brief order, Carter officially closed the case and canceled Friday's hearing.
