title: Why is Hegseth facing impeachment? Inside the 8 articles
summary: The impeachment resolution focuses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky is leading a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges are laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House is set to vote on whether to advance the articles at 5:30 p.m. on Tuesday.

The outcome is uncertain. Some Republicans are upset with the administration's handling of the Iran war, particularly given GOP losses in the midterm elections. House GOP leaders are vowing to defeat Massie's resolution, but attendance issues among members who lost their election could open the door for its passage.

The impeachment resolution focuses on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.
Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:
Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization
The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.
The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.
Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war
The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.
At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.
Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline
The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."
Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."
Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.
Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.
Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.
The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."
Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly
The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."
Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."
Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."
Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.
Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen
The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.
The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.
"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

title: House finds "decades-long failures" as Epstein preyed on victims
summary: The 15-month investigation by the House Oversight Committee involved interviews with some of Jeffrey Epstein's most high-powered associates.
story: The federal government failed for decades to stop Jeffrey Epstein as he manipulated and sexually abused young women and girls, despite growing evidence of his crimes, according to a report released Tuesday by Republicans on the House Oversight Committee.

The 15-month investigation involved 19 transcribed interviews with witnesses, including some of Epstein's most high-powered associates, and reviews of financial records, Justice Department documents and files from Epstein's estate.

"At nearly every stage, the cases reviewed by the Committee raise troubling questions about how Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, who sexually abused and trafficked young women and girls, avoided accountability for so long," the committee's majority wrote. Maxwell is a former socialite and convicted child sex trafficker who was among Epstein's closest confidants.

The committee's Republicans wrote that Epstein targeted vulnerable young women and girls, promising "career opportunities and comfort until the survivors of his crimes became completely dependent and subservient." Along the way, those around him "seemed to have simply blindly obeyed" as he manipulated the young women.
The committee's top Democrat, Robert Garcia, criticized the report, saying it's "based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings."

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation. We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started," Garcia said in a statement to press.

The report concluded that a "willful ignorance" extended from Epstein's closest employees — his longtime lawyer, accountant and personal assistant, who combined carried out the nitty gritty details of arranging daily massages and managing his "black book" of names — to Epstein's most powerful friends, "who, in the face of numerous red flags, claimed that they never suspected Epstein was abusing women or committing crimes of any kind."
But a willingness to allow Epstein's behavior to continue extended to the federal government itself, they wrote.

Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida state court in 2008 to two prostitution charges, including one count of soliciting prostitution from someone under 18. The report claims that this "sweetheart deal" allowed Epstein to avoid a more sweeping federal case, and may have resulted from conflicts of interest at the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, which ultimately decided against pushing federal charges.

During Epstein's short stint in state custody, he was granted extensive work-release for what the committee called a "sham company." During that time, he continued to abuse women, the committee wrote. Several survivors said they were abused during that time, "in his South Florida office, his Palm Beach residence, or even, in [Sarah] Kellen's case, over video from the stockade itself."

Epstein's fortune was enabled by a cadre of extraordinarily wealthy and powerful clients and friends. The committee interviewed, among others, billionaires Leon Black, Bill Gates, Les Wexner and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. They all said they had no knowledge of Epstein's crimes.

"Some Epstein associates questioned by the Committee seemingly claimed in their testimonies that a man with connections to global political leaders, major philanthropists, titans of industry, billionaires, Hollywood celebrities, and even a British prince could not be a sex trafficker," the committee wrote. "However, despite the repeated assertions of ignorance to Epstein's crimes, these same associates offered inadequate explanations for their continued close association with Epstein after his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor."
Black recently sued the committee's lead Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia, claiming defamation and accusing Garcia of lying about Black's relationship with Epstein.
Garcia said he intends to continue the investigation after Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"The Department of Justice continues to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents, there's been no investigation of Ghislaine Maxwell's transfer, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has yet to testify about his role in the largest government cover-up of the modern era," Garcia said, referring to the Justice Department's decision to move Maxwell to a minimum-security facility days after Blanche interviewed her. At the time, Blanche was deputy attorney general. It is extraordinarily unusual for Justice Department officials with that seniority to interview inmates.

The report's authors recommendations include encouraging the Justice Department pursue new investigations in Epstein's circle, and that Congress pass legislation to "prevent the weaponization of nondisclosure agreements to silence survivors of sexual abuse."

title: Dad went into "mission mode" to stop school shooting
summary: Kaylub Giamanco shared how he stopped a shooting at his daughters' school in Bend, Oregon, in his first network television interview.
story: The father who shot and killed a gunman at his daughters' Oregon school opened up about his experience in his first network television interview on "CBS Mornings," recounting the moment he fought with the shooter and how his heroic actions have affected him since.

Kaylub Giamanco, 36, was driving by Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 on his way home for lunch when he saw the shooter, later identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, fire at a passing pickup truck with a shotgun. The shooter then forced his way into the school, where Giamanco's two daughters are students.

"It was like fight or flight, and something clicked, and I just, I analyzed the situation. I knew something was up. All the emotions flood out of me. I just kind of went into a mission mode," Giamanco said.

Giamanco called 911 and said he was following the shooter into the building. He said he then crawled into the building and peeked into the classroom window, where he saw the gunman struggling with a teacher. She was unarmed, but had thrown her cellphone at the shooter and tackled him, according to police. Giamanco said that the teacher's intervention gave him "the split second of having two people side-by-side."
"I knew that he wasn't paying attention to me, so it gave me the opportunity to swing the door open and step in and complete my mission, so to speak," Giamanco said.

Giamanco said that after he shot the gunman the first time, the shooter was still alive, "struggling with his weapon" and "trying to regain control." The shooter was also trying to say something, Giamanco said, but he didn't listen.
"I didn't want to hear what he had to say. He had taken lives," Giamanco said. "I said 'F--- you.'"
"I don't know what he was about to say and it didn't matter," Giamanco added. "It didn't matter. I just knew he had taken the lives of innocent little babies, you know, 5, 8 and 11."
A teacher was also among those killed. Another teacher and a 7-year-old were injured in the shooting.

Giamanco said he dropped his gun once he confirmed the shooter was dead. He went to check on the other teacher, who "ran away from" him, he said. He said it wasn't "the greatest feeling," but that he understood she believed he might be another active shooter.
Then police arrived on the scene. Giamanco said he raised his hands and asked for help, then asked if he could pick up his weapon and go to his car to call his loved ones.

"During the situation I was not scared. Like I say, it was the fight mode that clicked in, and I completed my mission," Giamanco said. "It wasn't until I called my wife and my mother that everything kind of flooded in on me."
"Mixed feelings"

Kelsey Giamanco said she knew something was wrong even before her husband called her. She had been expecting him for lunch, so she had been following his location on her phone and noticed him stopped at the school. Kelsey Giamanco said she is usually the parent called for early pick-ups, so she didn't know what was going on. Once her husband called her and told her what had happened, she immediately drove to the school to meet him.
Kaylub Giamanco said that as the "gravity of the situation" hit him, he felt fear and had chest palpitations. Then, when he reunited with his children, there were "mixed feelings."

"I was really sad other people didn't get to hold their children that night ... but it felt good to just squeeze them and know that they were going to still be here and they could grow up to be, you know, beautiful young women," Giamanco said.
Talking to their children, who are 5 and 10, about what happened has been tricky, he said. He tries to reassure them that he is there to protect them.
"Our 10-year-old is very intellectual, so we have little conversations there, essentially just like, 'I just did what I felt was right,'" Giamanco said.

He is also still grappling with the event. Giamanco said he tries to distract himself and ride his motorcycle or dirt bikes as much as possible. But when he closes his eyes, he hears "children's screams and what it sounds like for them to plead for their life."

"I know exactly what that audio is in my brain," Giamanco said. "That's where, again, when I'm alone at nighttime and ready to go to bed, I don't always go to bed. Sometimes I get trapped in my brain."
Giamanco has not returned to his job as a carpenter. He said he is thinking about changing his career and might start a nonprofit for mental health and school security.
As he plans his future in the aftermath of the shooting, a famous quote from "Spider-Man" brings him some solace, he said.

"For me, when you are given these powers and you don't use them and someone gets hurt, then it is your fault. So I feel, to me, that means, if I have these abilities in life to be a protector, if I'm not using them and people do get hurt, that is my fault at the end of the day," Giamanco said. "It is kind of the same thing as 'With great powers come great responsibilities.' So I genuinely feel like I have something to do now."
This story published first on CBS News at 10:46 a.m. on Nov. 10, 2026.

title: Where the Trump administration's lawsuits seeking voter data stand
summary: The Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over their unredacted voter rolls containing voters' sensitive information.
story: Washington — President Trump's administration has mounted efforts in nearly all 50 states to obtain their complete voter rolls containing sensitive information about registered voters in their states.

The Justice Department has argued that the information is needed to ensure states are complying with two federal voting laws, the Help America Vote Act and the National Voter Registration Act, which aim to ensure states have programs in place for maintaining accurate voter rolls.

The administration sent letters to most of the states last year seeking unredacted electronic copies of their statewide voter registration lists, which include voters' birthdates, addresses, partial Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers.

A number of states have turned over publicly available versions of their voter rolls, but have declined to provide their complete lists. In response, the Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over the voter data.
So far, the Trump administration has lost 28 of those cases. Federal judges have rejected the Justice Department's lawsuits for unredacted voter rolls from:

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's initial case against Georgia because it was filed in the wrong court, and government lawyers then refiled it. The Justice Department voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against Oklahoma after the state agreed to turn over its voter registration list.
The other cases remain pending. Those are in Hawaii and Idaho.

The Justice Department has appealed most of the decisions dismissing its cases. So far, one appeals court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, has upheld a lower court decision rejecting the administration's attempt to obtain Michigan's voter rolls.

The Trump administration's bids to gain access to states' unredacted voter registration lists are part of the president's efforts to exert more power over federal elections. Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders aimed at U.S. elections, though both have been blocked by the courts.

The first executive order, signed last year, would require documentary proof of citizenship in order to register to vote. The second, announced in March, tightens the rules for mail-in voting and requires the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Postal Service to compile and maintain lists of U.S. citizens who are eligible to vote.
Mr. Trump is also pushing Congress to enact a package of voting regulations called the SAVE America Act, which would significantly curtail mail-in voting and impose new voter ID requirements.

The president has long taken aim at mail-in voting and claimed it leads to widespread fraud, though he has not put forth evidence in support of those claims. He has also claimed that Democratic states allow noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote.

title: Susie Wiles' old lobbying firm in crosshairs of MAGA feud
summary: Former top HHS aide Calley Means alleged in an interview with "Face the Nation" that Ballard Partners "controlled" White House policy. The firm and Wiles said the claims are false.
story: For the last two years, Brian Ballard's ties to President Trump made his lobbying firm one of the most sought-after in Washington. Now those same ties have made it a target in the Republican Party's post-midterm infighting.

Calley Means, a former top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., alleged in an interview Sunday with CBS News' "Face the Nation" that Ballard Partners "controlled" White House policy. Mr. Trump's former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, worked at the firm for nearly a decade as a managing partner, leaving in 2019.

Means claimed Ballard Partners' rise to become the top-earning lobbying firm "did not happen by accident." He accused Wiles and other top advisers to Mr. Trump of catering to industries that funded Republicans ahead of the midterms. Ballard and Wiles both called the claims false.
The firm's interactions with Wiles as chief of staff "have been limited and have been the exception, not the rule," Brian Ballard, a longtime Trump fundraiser, said in a rare statement Sunday.

Ballard Partners' more than $88 million in lobbying revenue last year was, at the time, the most any firm had reported since the Lobbying Disclosure Act took effect in 1996, even after adjusting for inflation, a CBS News analysis of Senate lobbying disclosures found. Through the first three quarters of 2026, the firm has already surpassed that, reporting more than $98 million.

The fortunes of Washington lobbying firms tend to rise and fall with changes in administrations, as companies hire them to try to influence policy. But after an election that saw government corruption polling as a top issue for voters, questions about who has profited from political connections are intensifying. Ballard Partners is now among those ensnared in the MAGA feud.

That tension could deepen ahead of 2028, as Republicans who cheered Mr. Trump's promise to "drain the swamp" speak out about the realities of an entrenched lobbying industry that has continued to thrive in Washington.

"The Democrats are going to start investigations as soon as they're sworn in, and White House fighting about who was making money will just elevate the topic," said Marc Short, a former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence.
The White House said in a statement that the Trump administration "has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions."
A fight over vapes

Brian Ballard has been one of Mr. Trump's top fundraisers for years, having reeled in $50 million for his campaign in 2024, according to a source familiar with the number who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Since 2008, he has chaired Florida finance committees for previous Republican presidential nominees. His firm opened a Washington office in 2017 and once employed both Wiles and Pam Bondi, who went on to serve as Mr. Trump's attorney general.

When Mr. Trump won a second term, the firm signed up hundreds of clients, though its relationship with the administration has seen ups and downs. For a brief period in 2025, Brian Ballard was banned from the West Wing after his firm's lobbying approach for a cryptocurrency client frustrated White House officials, two Trump advisers told CBS News. (Ballard apologized in May 2025 and returned to the White House's good graces, Axios reported.)
Among the firm's longest-standing clients is RAI Services Company, a subsidiary of tobacco giant Reynolds American. It has paid Ballard Partners millions of dollars since 2017, lobbying records show.

That relationship placed Ballard at the center of Means' allegations about favorable treatment for vaping interests. Means resigned in late October, claiming the Make America Healthy Again agenda had stalled in the White House. He placed the blame at Wiles' feet, saying she and "her deputies were still relentlessly pushing HHS to find a pathway for fruit-flavored vapes."

In May, the Food and Drug Administration handed the tobacco industry a win with new guidance that could let major tobacco companies sell flavored vapes. The announcement came a week after Brian Ballard and tobacco executives had lunch with Mr. Trump at his golf club in Jupiter, Florida, where the president called Kennedy and other health officials to complain about the FDA, The New York Times reported. The FDA decision also came after RAI Services Company had given $5 million to MAGA Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC, on April 30, Federal Election Commission records show. (FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned days after the guidance came out, in protest.) The White House has suggested the donation had nothing to do with the FDA decision.

In his statement Sunday, Ballard said no one at his firm advocated to Wiles or anyone at the White House on authorization for fruit-flavored vapes. He said his advocacy related to "illegal, unregulated vapes from China," some of which, he said, have been found to be laced with fentanyl.
Wiles told CBS News she had nothing to do with the tobacco industry meeting with Mr. Trump at his golf club.

Means also singled out James Blair, the former deputy chief of staff, claiming he was "relentless on helping the fruit-flavored vape industry." Blair, who left the White House in April to oversee the GOP's midterm strategy, has traded barbs with Means on social media, calling the claim that he pushed vapes as a core midterm issue "a complete and total lie."

"I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair told CBS News, adding that he was tasked with making sure the FDA ruled on nicotine product applications swiftly – within six months. "Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely," Blair added.

Blair spoke with Reynolds and other vape companies about the FDA's application process, but not about any specific applications or products, according to two sources familiar with the conversations who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Blair has said he is reviewing his legal options and whether to sue Means for defamation.

A MAGA Inc. spokesperson said the group "is pleased to accept legal contributions from those who agree with President Trump's America First agenda." A spokesperson for Wiles told Axios that Means' accusations of corruption were "outrageous, defamatory, and provably false."
"What Ballard helps you do"

Means' accusations centered on what he called a "very close-knit crew" around Wiles that "explicitly catered to special interests." He alleged that the goal was to serve big business interests in exchange for money for the midterms. Steering those donations, he alleged, "is what Ballard helps you do."

Lobbying firms in Washington routinely advise clients on political giving, and many lobbyists raise money for candidates themselves. The practice is legal, though federal law requires lobbyists to disclose their own contributions twice a year.

Means also pointed to a long-running dispute about glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, which has been linked to cancer. He accused administration officials of siding with Bayer, which makes Roundup, by formally supporting the company's argument at the Supreme Court to block state lawsuits over the herbicide. A White House official told CBS News that Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote a brief at the court's request.

Bayer has paid Ballard Partners since January 2024 to lobby Congress and the administration on a number of issues, according to lobbying disclosures. Ballard said no one at the firm lobbied Wiles or West Wing staff on glyphosate.

Means' claim that Wiles was hostile to the MAHA agenda has drawn pushback from her allies. Two sources, who requested anonymity to describe a private meeting, recounted a White House meeting last year in which an administration official derided MAHA supporters as "nuts." Wiles shot back: "I'm one of those MAHA nuts," the sources said.
A White House official told CBS News that Wiles "has been an essential leader in Making America Healthy Again."

Mr. Trump's longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio, whom Means accused of working to help pharmaceutical interests, said in a statement that Means' allegation that he is "in the pocket of Big Pharma" was "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false." Fabrizio previously urged Republicans to campaign on lowering prescription drug prices, finding in an April 2025 poll that the issue could give GOP candidates in toss-up districts a 20-point boost.

The fight is unlikely to fade soon. California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said he will look into the claims against Wiles. Attorney General Todd Blanche has dismissed Means as a "disgruntled former administration official," and told CNN the Justice Department would not investigate "something that someone says on a podcast."

title: FDA warns of rare vision-loss side effect from GLP-1 drugs
summary: The Food and Drug Administration is adding a new warning about possible rare cases of vision loss reported with GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy and other brands.
story: Popular weight loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy, will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday.

The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.

The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.

FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy.

Dr. Joseph Rizzo, a neuro-ophthalmologist at Massachusetts Eye and Ear who co-authored that paper, told CBS News on Monday that he and his team had been working with the FDA to gather and review data on the issue for some time and that, while he didn't know the agency was ready to make a decision, he wasn't surprised it chose to add the warning.

He stressed that while he believes the evidence shows GLP-1 usage increases the risk of developing NAION, he doesn't discourage patients from taking them, saying, "The medicines have really been profoundly beneficial to a large number of people."
People who aren't on GLP-1s can also develop NAION, which affects somewhere between 2 to 10 of every 100,000 adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.

Novo Nordisk, the maker of Wegovy and Ozempic, said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines."

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families," it said. "Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines, review new research and work with health authorities around the world."
Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound and Mounjaro, said in a statement Monday it was "carefully evaluating the update and will respond to FDA promptly."

"Patient safety is Lilly's top priority," the company said. "FDA's drug safety communication applies to all medicines with GLP-1 RA activity and does not reference any findings specific to Lilly medicines."

An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.

Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a healthcare professional immediately, the agency said.
Rizzo noted that the vision loss from the condition tends to be irreversible and can become progressively worse, even if a patient stops taking the medication.

"Usually when you lose vision, although there may be some mild degree of improvement, it's usually not a large degree of improvement," he said. "And unfortunately, a great frustration for so many of our patients and doctors who take care of patients with NAION  is the fact that we do not really know how to mitigate the risk."
Rizzo also said the condition does not necessarily affect each eye the same.

"The degree of visual loss in the first eye does not inform the degree of visual loss that would occur in the second eye," he told CBS News. "So you could have mild visual loss in one eye, and then the next eye could be severe."

title: Massie introduces Hegseth impeachment articles, teeing up vote
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.
story: Washington — Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and abusing the powers of his office.

The impeachment effort could attract more bipartisan support, since members of both parties are frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran and Republicans are reeling from their defeats in the midterm elections. Lawmakers returned to Capitol Hill on Monday to reconvene for the final weeks of the GOP-controlled Congress, and Massie's move will force leaders to bring the impeachment resolution up for a vote within two legislative days.

Even before the midterm elections highlighted voters' concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living, the push to impeach Hegseth was underway in Congress. Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has broken with the administration on a number of fronts over the past year, originally introduced impeachment articles against the defense secretary in September. House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.
Massie introduced updated impeachment articles on the House floor on Monday, restarting a two-day clock for GOP leaders to schedule a vote.

The Kentucky Republican accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanours in a 34-page impeachment resolution with eight articles. Three charges accuse him of abusing the powers of the Department of Defense by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.

Massie also alleged that in the conflict, Hegseth ignored laws that minimize civilian casualties, citing the strike on an Iranian school earlier this year. Another impeachment article points to the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, while one cites the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Another centers on free speech and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly after he was among a group of lawmakers who released a video calling on service members to "refuse illegal orders."

Massie argued that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," Massie wrote.

Massie urged the GOP-controlled Senate to take up the resolution if it passes the House, noting that the articles will survive into the next Congress, when the upper chamber has a Democratic majority.

"If the Senate doesn't deal with this before the end of this Senate, they're turning it over to a Democrat Senate who can then have the trials and deal with it," Massie said at a news conference Monday afternoon.
Massie argued he was being "polite" with the impeachment effort and that "when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

"What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don't go to prison. You don't go to jail. You don't pay a fine," he said. "But the Democrats are going to have hearings. They won't have just eight articles of impeachment. … The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection."
Hegseth has criticized the effort by Massie, who's leaving Congress after losing his primary earlier this year.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in a video posted on X last week. "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Hegseth told reporters Monday, "we're not worried about that." He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.

Whether other Republicans support the effort remains to be seen. But some GOP members appeared more open to the prospect, and more eager to criticize the defense secretary, after the brutal losses for their party in the midterms.
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, said on News Nation that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer said. "I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas indicated that he's still considering whether to support the effort, saying on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that he wants to hear the debate on the issue "to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the administration on some issues, said he's "wrestling" with whether to support the impeachment resolution.
He said Hegseth's handling of a number of topics "bothers me" and "I feel like he deserves a little bit of his own treatment, but that's not the right way to handle impeachment."
"I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor," Bacon told reporters Monday at the Capitol.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said Monday that impeaching Hegseth amid hostilities abroad "would be a terrible, terrible look."

Democrats are widely expected to support the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment effort. But with a narrow GOP majority, Republican votes will be needed.

Massie said in a post on X on Monday that he's seen some of his colleagues say "Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they'll vote not to impeach." But he said "that's not the question."
"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie said. "And the answer is yes, eight times."

Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 over corruption allegations. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by the GOP-controlled House in 2024 over the Biden administration's handling of the southern border. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate. Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

title: Trump admin. proposes stricter unemployment work search rules
summary: Under a proposed federal rule, Americans seeking unemployment aid would have to conduct more job searches each week.
story: The Trump administration on Monday proposed stiffer rules for Americans seeking unemployment benefits that, if adopted, would require them to conduct more weekly job searches.

The proposed Department of Labor regulations, set to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, would require people applying for or collecting jobless aid to complete at least five unique work searches per week. Currently, many U.S. states require two to three qualifying work searches per week, while only four states require five. Some states require only one work search activity to qualify for unemployment benefits.

The Trump administration said the change is necessary to create consistent eligibility requirements for unemployment benefits nationwide. A national minimum weekly work search standard would "improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment," the Labor Department said in its proposal.

"This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work," according to the agency. "The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering [an unemployment compensation] program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market."
The public has 60 days following publication of the proposed rule to offer comment.
Costly for states and workers
Labor advocates criticized the proposed change in work search rules, saying the new threshold would be hard for unemployed people to meet and costly for states to administer.

"Not only is the proposed change devastating to claimants who may not have five search options for every week they are unemployed, but it will likely cost states hundreds of thousands of dollars," Michele Evermore, senior director of economic security and worker transitions at the National Employment Law Project, a worker advocacy group, said in a statement to CBS News. "Nearly all states will have to change their claimant intake forms, and with it, their technology — a costly fix. Many states will have to rewrite their laws to meet this rule."

Evermore also said the proposed rule would disadvantage applicants who already struggle to navigate the unemployment benefits systems. Employers "want candidates enthusiastic about their job opportunities, not ticking boxes for the work search form," she added.
More level playing field?

The Labor Department acknowledged that the policy could temporarily raise costs as states and jobless aid applicants adapt to the new work requirement, but said the change is necessary to ensure that the eligibility rules are applied consistently across the U.S.

"These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear," the Labor Department said. "Additionally, variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules."

Various activities would satisfy the proposed requirement that people seeking jobless aid conduct at least five work searches per week, according to the Labor Department. For example, beyond contacting a prospective employer, registering with or contacting a job placement agency or union would also count as a qualified work search.

Under the proposal, states could also designate other activities as satisfying the requirement. Additionally, states could adapt the weekly job search threshold to account for local labor market conditions through a points-based system that would allow someone applying for jobless aid to accrue multiple points for a single activity.
"Under such a system, States may assign point values to qualifying work search activities and require individuals to accumulate a minimum of five points per benefit week," the Labor Department said.

title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
summary: It was reported in October that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.

Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.
Allegations in Philippines lead to U.S. and Mexican investigations

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."
The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.
In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."
DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.
Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."
If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.
According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.

title: Frantic 911 call from hero dad who killed school shooter released
summary: The armed father who was hailed for his heroic actions​ during a deadly shooting​ at his daughters' elementary school in Oregon frantically called authorities before he went after the shooter.
story: The armed father who was hailed for his heroic actions during a deadly shooting at his daughters' elementary school in Oregon frantically called authorities before he went after the shooter, according to a recording of the 911 call released Tuesday.

"Someone's at the school, at my daughters' school with a gun. I have a gun, and I will shoot them right now if I have to," 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 dispatcher as the Oct. 15 shooting was beginning to unfold.

Giamanco's two daughters were inside Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, when he happened to drive by the school and see the shooter begin his rampage. Giamanco's girls survived the attack.
The shooter killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Giamanco killed the 16-year-old shooter after rushing into the school with his handgun.

The roughly 80-second-long recording released Tuesday captures the initial chaos surrounding the shooting, which started when the gunman shot at a vehicle. Giamanco previously told Oregon Public Broadcasting he went for his gun in a panic after he saw the shooter throw his weapon over the school's fence and then climb after it.
Giamanco's first words on the 911 call were, "Oh my God."
After Giamanco described the situation to the dispatcher, the dispatcher asked exactly what happened.
"Silver Rail Elementary! Silver Rail Elementary!" Giamanco told her.
The dispatcher asked Giamanco for his phone number and then if he knew who the shooter was.
"This is my daughters' school. I'm about to go kill this kid," Giamanco said.
The dispatcher asked again if he knew the shooter's identity.
"No, I don't f---ing know, I was just driving," Giamanco said.

Giamanco then told the dispatcher the shooter was inside the school. The dispatcher asked where. Giamanco again gave the name of the school. When the dispatcher asked where the shooter was located in the school, he provided additional details.
"God d--- it, they're f---ing shooting people. Come on!" Giamanco said.
The call ends shortly after the dispatcher asked for a description of the shooter.
"Sir, I need you to tell me what's going on," the dispatcher said. "We have help en route."

title: Jockey Izzy Neale, 22, dies after her horse falls during race
summary: Izzy Neale suffered injuries when her horse Marnoo fell and suffered a fatal leg injury in the homestretch of a 1-mile race.
story: Jockey Izzy Neale died on Tuesday, two days after her horse fell during a race in Australia, the Racing NSW state thoroughbred authority said.
The 22-year-old Neale suffered injuries Sunday when her horse Marnoo fell and suffered a fatal leg injury in the homestretch of a 1-mile race at Warren racecourse.
She was unconscious when airlifted to a hospital, and Racing NSW released a statement Tuesday from her family that she had died.

"Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing," the statement said of Neale, who rode 88 winners in her career.
"Through organ donation, Izzy will give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to our family amid this devastating loss."
Rider Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse during the race, Racing NSW said in a statement, adding that he suffered a foot injury but was later discharged from the hospital.
Neale had 699 career starts in her career, local media reported.

Her brother Tommy Neale wrote on Facebook that he couldn't "believe what's happened," adding: "You'll always be my lil baby sister, you were my best friend an we always was so close so I dunno how I'm gonna deal with this."

title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
summary: The Paris prosecutor's office says investigators have determined that a cyberattack on grocery store chains was "carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran."
story: French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country."

The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.

The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.

In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News. Hamilton told CBS News this week that the division's Cyber Field Office was working with French law enforcement to understand the refrigeration outages in Europe.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.

In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

It said the alleged offenses were "further aggravated by the fact that they were carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran — in addition to participation in a criminal conspiracy to prepare for the commission of a serious crime (felony)."

According to the allegations, the investigation is targeting the leader of an Iranian group known as "Shahid Kaveh," which the prosecutor's office described as "a cyber-offensive unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-ECC) — as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who may be identified."

"The attackers gained remote control of the equipment via web interfaces, initiating indefinite, abnormal defrost cycles while simultaneously disabling safety alerts — alerts designed to trigger when temperatures exceeded specific thresholds," the prosecutor's office said, adding that the probe had "uncovered an attack methodology characteristic of this [Iranian] unit, including the use of the Persian (Farsi) language and IP addresses that trace back to devices located in Iran."
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Tuesday that the country "rules nothing out" in terms of its response to the cyberattack.
"This is a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country," Barrot told French broadcaster Franceinfo.
"We are going to summon the [Iranian] ambassador and will call for European sanctions," he said, adding that "we will not stop at merely" those measures in response.
Barrot called the cyberattack "a major threat to the security of the French people" and said the government was "taking every measure to deter any further attacks."

Later Tuesday, the foreign ministry reitterated most of Barrot's remarks, and said in a statement that the hack was "unprecedented in its scale and level of aggressiveness and has been the first offensive cyber campaign carried out purely for the purposes of sabotage on French soil."

In a statement shared on social media last week, the FBI's cybercrime branch said that, along with its partners, it was "seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world," noting that "security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage."

The FBI urged all organizations that rely on such systems to take their controllers "off the public internet" and to keep access to the systems behind a firewall, in addition to other security measures.

There was no immediate response from Iranian authorities to the allegations by the French prosecutor on Monday, but the regime has threatened for months to expand its retaliation for the war launched by the U.S., and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its ports, using unspecified, asymmetrical means.
CBS News' Karine Barzegar contributed to this report.

title: Reported Iran threat sees U.S. move planes from second U.K. base
summary: The reported movement comes just over a month after a security incident at a separate air base hosting U.S. aircraft used in the war with Iran.
story: The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.
It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.
A U.S. official told CBS News later Tuesday that there were credible threats against bases in the U.K., without specifying who was behind the threats.

CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany.
Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain.

"We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements.

Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.

A spokesperson for the U.S. military's European Command said they could not comment on "specific force protection measures," adding that, "in close partnership with our host nation allies, both RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath remain vigilant" and that along with U.K. authorities, "we are taking coordinated and appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families."

A U.S. Air Force spokesperson told CBS News earlier Tuesday that aircraft routinely "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements."

The spokesman added that "U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets."

The U.S. Air Force 100th Air Refueling Wing, which has been based at RAF Mildenhall for years, did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment on the aircraft movements. The 100th air wing is the only permanent U.S. refueling wing in Europe.

The relocation of the aircraft comes just over a month after the U.S. Air Force decided to remove all of its long-range bombers from RAF Fairford, another air base in England that had been used to launch strikes on Iran, following a security incident there.

On Sept. 27, five British men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses close to the Fairford base. The suspects were later released on bail. A month later, two men were charged with security-related offenses in connection with the incident.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

Nouman Essghir, also 24, was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the time that Iran was believed to have "played a part" in the September incident, though he did not provide any details.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham told the BBC in October.

U.K. counterterrorism police said no explosives were found in extensive searches of the three vehicles operated by the men arrested near RAF Fairford, only some fuel and a number of large, mostly empty plastic drums.

title: No sign of progress as U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks get underway
summary: It is the first such trilateral diplomatic push since negotiations were suspended following the start of the war with Iran.
story: The United States, Ukraine and Russia held their first round of trilateral talks in about nine months Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, aimed at ending the war that started when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of the neighboring nation.

After the first of two days of talks set to focus on security guarantees — a long-running demand from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — it was clear neither side expected an imminent breakthrough, but Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive."

President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said in a post on X ahead of the meetings that he and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were "working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."

Kushner indicated this round of talks in the United Arab Emirates capital was just an initial step, but one he said could "build momentum" toward future negotiations. He also suggested a future agreement would involve a security arrangement involving European countries and Russia.
But Russia and Ukraine seemed to pour cold water on the initiative after Tuesday's round of talks.

Russia's veteran Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow rejected European demands for a ceasefire in Ukraine, accusing Brussels, where the European Union is based, of trying to "buy time" for Kyiv.
"We will not agree to this," he said.
Lavrov said Moscow does not want to prevent the U.S. from engaging with Europe on the Ukraine war, but Russia does not consider it to be the best approach.

Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram, meanwhile, that the U.S. had asked if Kyiv would be willing to "trade the Donbas for security," referring to a vast eastern region of Ukraine that Russia has largely occupied by force. So far, Ukraine has insisted it should be allowed to keep the region as part of a peace deal. But he said in exchange for the proposed territorial concession, the U.S. was not willing to accept that Ukraine should become a member of the NATO alliance, instead suggesting Kyiv should settle for "something similar."
"No one believes that Putin will stop if we give up the Donbas," Zelenksyy said. "He might pause — but then he will return in a year, two years or five years. And who will be to blame then?"

In a subsequent statement, also shared online, Zelenskyy called the first round constructive and said the two sides had "managed to discuss the necessity and possible parameters of humanitarian measures," including another possible mutual release of prisoners of war.

"We discussed in detail the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for their long-term effectiveness," he said, adding that Ukraine needed "practical mechanisms to prevent any recurrence of the war."

Putin has previously said he wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, the four regions of the Donbas that Moscow illegally declared its territory in September 2022, but never fully captured. He has also long demanded that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Zelenskyy has consistently rejected Putin's demands to cede territory Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy has also rejected any limits being placed on Ukraine's military, or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

The U.S., Russia and Ukraine have held three other rounds of trilateral talks this year — the first in January and second in February — but diplomatic efforts largely stalled after President Trump decided to launch, alongside Israel, the ongoing war with Iran. Since then, Witkoff and Kushner have held various separate meetings with Putin and Zelenskyy.

In October, first lady Melania Trump's office said she had secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons. It lasted from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1.

title: Meghan and Harry do first public event since her father's arrest
summary: Harry and Meghan's first appearance since the duchess's estranged father was arrested over alleged child sex abuse imagery was at an EU event on online safety for kids.
story: London — Prince Harry and Meghan held hands tightly Tuesday as they stepped into public view for the first time since the Duchess of Sussex's estranged father was arrested in the United States. The FBI detained Thomas Markle Sr., 82, in Florida on Friday after federal prosecutors charged him the previous day with possession of images of child sexual abuse.

Harry and Meghan arrived Tuesday at the European Parliament in Brussels for an event focused on online child safety. Harry and Meghan had been slated to deliver a keynote speech together at the Lost Screen Memorial, but Meghan withdrew, leaving Harry to address the event solo.
Children "deserve to feel safe wherever they are," Harry said, standing alone at the podium, "in a classroom. On a playground. At any time, no matter where they are."

The scheduled event's focus was on addressing the perils of online abuse and exploitation of children, but Harry's remarks carried deeper significance for his wife and all those in attendance given the timing.

"I know from people close to her that she is very, very emotional, and that is the reason why she pulled out of giving the speech along with Harry today in Brussels," said Roya Nikkhah, royal editor of Britain's Sunday Times newspaper and a CBS News contributor. "It's been a very difficult time for her."
Nikkhah said Meghan had decided to still attend the event in "solidarity," which she called "a strong indication of how strongly and passionately she feels" about the subject matter.

The duchess said last month that she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations against her father, and that she had first heard "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018, which she said had played a large part in her and William's decision to keep him from their own children.

"I think for her, she's trying to process it," said Nikkhah. "Trying to protect her children as well, and maintain some sort of semblance of normal family life, but from what I understand, that's very difficult at the moment."

According to an FBI affidavit, investigators found dozens of items including slides, film negatives and books at two storage units in Los Angeles, with some photographs appearing to show Thomas Markle Sr. with children in "various stages of undress."
Police in the Philippines confirmed in late October that they are also investigating alleged child sexual abuse materials found at Markle's former home in the city of Cebu.
Markle has denied any wrongdoing and dismissed some of the allegations as "sick lies."

"Meghan is very keen to cooperate with the FBI investigation and any other investigations around the world," said Nikkhah on Tuesday. "I was told she would very much like to help those investigations, provide any evidence or help that she can, so that is very much her plan."
She added, however, that it would not be straightforward for the duchess.

"That is going to be something else that she will need to navigate," she said, adding that the royal couple are "keen not to stop all of their public work, and try and carry on in any way that they can."

Harry and Meghan's appearance at the European Parliament was also their first public event since they returned to the U.K. over the summer after spending more than six years living in the United States.

A U.S. judge ordered Markle to undergo a psychiatric evaluation last week, setting a deadline of Nov. 20, saying there was "reasonable cause to believe" he may be "mentally incompetent" to stand trial.
Markle is living at a nursing home in Lakeland, Florida, under police watch and house arrest.

title: Congo court sentences 66 soldiers to death for cowardice, mutiny
summary: A military court in the Democratic Republic of Congo has sentenced 66 soldiers to death for cowardice and mutiny after they allegedly fled fighting with rebels.
story: A military court in the Democratic Republic of Congo has sentenced 66 soldiers to death for cowardice, refusing to obey orders, mutiny and squandering of munition, according to local media reports. The troops spent 12 days on trial at a military court in the town of Walikale, in Congo's eastern North Kivu province, according to Radio Okapi, along with four others who were acquitted and one who was given a 10-year jail sentence.
Military authorities said the aim of the trial was to boost discipline in the armed forces, according to multiple reports by Congolese and international news outlets.

Troops from Congo have been fighting armed groups in the country's resource-rich east for decades, including the M23 group, and the umbrella rebel coalition Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN).
The soldiers were arrested on Oct. 20 after being accused of fleeing fighting with FRN fighters, according to CBS News' partner network BBC News.
The country's armed forces have been plagued by accusations of ill-discipline, while soldiers have decried poor pay and equipment, according to the BBC.
In early October, 27 other Congolese government soldiers were sentenced to death for cowardice, Radio Okapi reported.

Congolese authorities reintroduced the death penalty in March 2024 to fight "treason" within the armed forces, according to Amnesty International, which, at the time, said the country's justice system was "plagued by numerous problems, and trials rarely meet fair trial standards as documented."

"Whether those who have been sentenced to death are in the national army or police, in armed groups or have been involved in gang violence, everyone has a right to life and for that right to be protected," Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty's regional director for East and Southern Africa, said. "This heartless decision will endanger the lives of hundreds of people who have been sentenced to death, including those who were put on death row following unfair trials and politically motivated charges."

The United Nations, many Western governments and the DRC have long accused the government in neighboring Rwanda of backing M23 in a bid to control and exploit the much larger country's vast mineral resources.
The United Nations warned last year the M23 fighters were carrying out summary executions and mass rape as they advanced into DR Congo.
Since the start of 2025, 381 Congolese soldiers have been sentenced to death, according to a tally by Radio France Internationale.
