"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

title: Mamdani makes behind-the-scenes moves to shape 2028 Democratic presidential race
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is meeting with labor leaders to rally progressives around a 2028 presidential candidate if AOC stays out.
story: Asked about 2028, progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York brushes aside political speculation, says voters want Democrats in Congress focused on governing.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is quietly working towards a new goal: to become a progressive kingmaker in the burgeoning battle for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

The socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, who can't run for president himself because he's not a natural-born U.S. citizen, has been meeting behind closed doors with labor leaders to highlight the need for a union-aligned or left-wing candidate to seek the presidency.
The mayor's moves come as he's reportedly said he's uncertain whether progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, his close political ally, will run for the White House.

According to Axios, which was first to report the news, Mamdani is concerned that if Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it could leave progressives without a standard-bearer to face off against a more centrist presidential frontrunner in the primary battle.
WILL TRUMP SIT OUT MAKING A 2028 ENDORSEMENT IN THE RACE TO SUCCEED HIM?
Then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani holds hands with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the end of a campaign rally in Queens on Oct. 26, 2025. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

Mamdani, who is seen as a major powerbroker for the left wing of the Democratic Party after his historic 2025 mayoral election victory, argues that the progressive movement can't waste its momentum coming out of last week's trouncing of Republicans in the midterm elections, as Democrats won a massive House majority and control of the Senate.

A source familiar with Mamdani's 2028 conversations told Axios the mayor "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise,"

Meanwhile, Ocasio-Cortez is publicly pumping the brakes on speculation she'll launch a presidential campaign or bid for the Senate in New York, even as a newly formed group of activists is urging her run for the White House.
VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I think the thing that's important here is the last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election. And what they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters Monday night, pointing to the midterms.

The comments from Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected last week to a fifth term representing parts of New York City, came hours after the formal launch of Ready for AOC, a political group working to encourage her to run for president by showing her she has legions of supporters ready to mobilize on her behalf.
"A people-powered movement asking Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for President in 2028. No campaign. No money. Just names," is how the group described itself on social media.
But Ocasio-Cortez said voters are more concerned about congressional Democrats' immediate legislative agenda rather than speculating about the next election.

"I think people are less concerned about the horse race, and they want to know: What are the investigations we're going to be starting? What is the legislation that we're going to be starting?" she said.

Veteran Democratic strategist David Plouffe, campaign manager for former President Barack Obama's landmark 2008 White House victory and a senior advisor on then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 bid, said last week, "If AOC runs, she's going to start, 20-25%, probably. The question is, can she add to that? If she doesn't run, then that is wide open. That's where I think someone like Abdul may say, 'Even though I just won, should I look at it?'"
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Abdul El-Sayed celebrates his victory during an election night event with Michigan Democrats in Detroit, Nov. 4, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Plouffe, who was speaking at a forum hosted by Harvard University's Institute of Politics, was referring to Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who made history last week as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
"That's the thing about this race. It's so wide open that there may be some people run who surprise us. I also think there'll be some people who don't run who'll surprise us," Plouffe added.

Ocasio-Cortez said in September that she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a White House run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker.
"I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email to supporters.

The now-37-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a New York Times interview two months ago that her decision, which could happen sometime after the midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?"
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speak on Capitol Hill on Aug. 3, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for sixth six-year term in the Senate.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ocasio-Cortez isn't the only leading figure on the left who is mulling a presidential run. So is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a top House progressive.
Allies of the soon-to-be six-term congressman last week launched a draft committee called "Run Ro" to build support and raise funds for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Cornyn meets with Sen-elect Talarico, describes him as 'basically ... a good person'
summary: Sen. John Cornyn meets with Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas and D.C. after the Democrat's massive win against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a U.S. Senate contest.
story: Texas Senator-elect James Talarico joins 'America's Newsroom' to outline his plans to work across the aisle, expressing support for President Trump's efforts on border security and highlighting the need for comprehensive housing solutions.
Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, has said that he met with Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico in Washington, D.C., on Monday after previously meeting with him on Friday in Texas.
"Good meeting with Senator-elect @jamestalarico today as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate next Congress," Cornyn said in a post on X which features a photo of the two men shaking hands.
Talarico also shared the photo in a post on X and commented on their meeting.
TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET
Senator-elect James Talarico shakes hands with Sen. John Cornyn. (Office of U.S. Senator John Cornyn)

"I just met with Senator John Cornyn. He has served our state honorably, and I’m grateful for his advice and guidance. Now is the time for us to come together — Democrats and Republicans — to deliver for Texas," Talarico wrote.

Cornyn said that he thinks Talarico is "basically ... a good person," telling reporter Nicholas Ballasy on Monday that he "enjoyed meeting with" Talarico "last Friday in Austin and again this morning here in D.C."
JAMES TALARICO BLAMES RISE IN GOP 'EXTREMISM' FOR PROMPTING HIS 'GOD IS NON-BINARY,' SIX SEXES REMARKS
President Donald Trump looks on as Ken Paxton speaks at a campaign rally at Lubbock Memorial Civic Center on Oct. 27, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

title: Progressive org launches campaign urging AOC to run for president while progressives eye socialist candidate
summary: Ready for AOC launched a nationwide signature drive urging Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028 as DSA allies eye a socialist nominee.
story: Asked about 2028, progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York brushes aside political speculation, says voters want Democrats in Congress focused on governing.

A progressive organization urging Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 has kicked off a campaign to collect signatures nationwide in support of the congresswoman's potential run.

Ready for AOC, which describes itself as a "people-powered," "grassroots" and "unaffiliated" organization, launched the campaign Monday, urging supporters of the congresswoman to ask her to run for president.
"Movements like this work when they're loud and early — long before the candidate says yes. The proof isn't money. It's names. Yours makes the case louder," the campaign's website states.
WATCH: AOC LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID: 'MAYBE, MAYBE NOT'

The website boasts 804 signatures as of Tuesday morning, though representatives for the project claim to be aiming for 10,000 community leaders to join their mission, according to the New York Times. The group also claims to have 500 political and union leaders across 35 states on board, the outlet reported.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in July. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"The goal is to build the infrastructure of a grassroots movement in the case that she decides to run, but also to demonstrate to her that, ‘Look, there is a movement behind you ready to power you to victory should you choose to run for president,'" Ravi Sahai, a spokesman for the group, told the New York Times.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Ocasio-Cortez herself has been coy about a potential run, but hasn't ruled it out. Asked by Fox News Digital in July if she'd consider running, she replied, "I have genuinely not really weighed seriously anything past the midterm elections."

However, following a sweeping blue wave in the midterms that saw voters punch ballots for numerous members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and other far-left candidates, the DSA's ranks are emboldened by the results and vocally making the case that America is ready for a far-left president.
MEET THE FAR-LEFT SOCIALISTS COMING TO CONGRESS NEXT YEAR

"For so long, we have been told that democratic socialists would be a liability," Gustavo Gordillo, the co-chair of New York City's DSA, said while speaking at an Astoria, Queens watch party on election night. "We've been told for so long that if we elect democratic socialists throughout the country that we won't be able to win races in Texas, in Florida. Tonight, we actually elected a democratic socialist in Tampa in a Republican MAGA-held seat," he bragged, according to state outlet City & State New York.

The DSA, which will hold a citywide convention in New York on Nov. 14, will hold a vote on whether the organization will formally push for Ocasio-Cortez to run, Gordillo revealed to a crowd at the watch party, City & State reported.
FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez speaks to members of the media in 2025. (Reuters/Jeenah Moon)
Despite the buzz, however, Ocasio-Cortez has downplayed speculation following the election, telling reporters that Democrats need to focus on governing over running.

"The last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician is about the next election. What they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," she told reporters Monday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, arguably the DSA's biggest success story, recently told NBC that America is "absolutely" ready for a socialist president.

"We have heard time and again over the 10 months that I've been in office here in New York City, that what we're doing here can't work elsewhere, that what people are concerned about here isn't what people are concerned about across the country," Mamdani told NBC's Kristen Welker the day after Election Day. "And what we saw last night is that the struggles of Americans in Atlanta, of Americans in Allentown, are not all that different than the struggles of Americans in Astoria."
AOC OPENS UP ABOUT RACE, GENDER IN WEIGHING POSSIBLE 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID

Mamdani, who was frequently joined by Ocasio-Cortez while campaigning for mayor in 2025, has not specifically mentioned any potential 2028 candidate by name, but is reportedly meeting with labor and union leaders to organize a potential progressive bloc for 2028.
Mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani holds hands with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the end of a campaign rally in Queens, New York, Oct. 26, 2025. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

Ocasio-Cortez was tabbed as the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee in a July poll from New Hampshire Granite State, however a more recent poll from Atlas Insights had her tied with Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.
WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Other potential Democratic candidates being eyeballed as would-be nominees include former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif.
Fox News Digital contacted  Ocasio-Cortez, Ready for AOC and the Democratic Socialists of America for further comment.

title: Nvidia spy case exposes how foreign agents target America’s corporate elite: 'He is compromised'
summary: Nvidia's CEO apologized to employees for infidelity as the board launched an independent probe into his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer called for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to step down, saying his reported relationship with a woman identified as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset raises national security concerns.
Nvidia’s reported spy scandal is shaking markets and rattling the tech world, raising urgent questions about how close foreign agents can get to America’s most powerful corporate leaders.

Dr. Michael Wallace, a professor at Tulane University and retired military intelligence officer with 20 years of experience, said foreign intelligence services study targets’ personal lives and interests to find ways to build trust and gain access.

And it's become increasingly clear that business leaders worldwide could potentially provide access or information about the U.S. government if placed correctly. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was on Air Force One with President Donald Trump in May as part of the delegation during a summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. He has also visited the White House a handful of times to discuss the administration's artificial intelligence (AI) agenda and Nvidia's powerful chips and selling them to approved Chinese customers.
HOW US CEOS QUIETLY TEAMED UP WITH TRUMP TO GAIN LEVERAGE OVER CHINA
Graphic labels key CEOs in attendance at a high-profile meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese officials. (Official White House Photo by Daniel Torok/Fox News)

There are now active investigations into whether U.S. national security or company secrets were compromised by Huang’s reported extramarital affair with a businesswoman allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to target the Nvidia CEO.
"The goal of human intelligence is to get somebody close to a source that can either elicit information or obtain information from a person," Wallace told Fox News Digital.

That access could reveal more than technical secrets, Wallace said. Someone close to a CEO might learn about business relationships, product plans, upcoming chip releases or conversations with government officials.

The allegations revive longstanding U.S. concerns about Chinese corporate espionage and efforts to gain access to American companies’ sensitive technology and business information. Those concerns carry added weight in Nvidia’s case because its advanced chips are central to the artificial intelligence industry and the U.S.-China technology competition.
NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG APOLOGIZES AS FIRM PROBES AFFAIR WITH ALLEGED SPY

Jensen Huang apologized to Nvidia employees for being unfaithful to his wife, saying his actions hurt her and their children and that "there is no excuse for what I did." (Soeren Stache/picture alliance/Getty Images)
"What makes it unique is that it happened this high up to this person," Wallace said. "That’s what boggles my mind."

Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into reports about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. Alice, despite sharing a last name, has no relation to the Nvidia CEO.

The New York Times reported that U.S. officials suspected Alice had gathered information for Beijing. Nvidia has said Huang meets with thousands of customer executives each year and that meetings with her were not unusual.
The news caused shock waves across business and government, and is leading to calls for Huang to resign.
HOUSE REPUBLICANS DEMAND ANSWERS FROM NVIDIA CEO OVER REPORTED CHINESE SPY TIES

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China, making the company’s technology a focal point in the U.S.-China race for AI leadership. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Huang apologized to Nvidia employees Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife, writing, "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." He did not identify the woman or describe the relationship in his message.

The board said independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would oversee the inquiry. It said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," while adding that the investigation would examine all available information. Nvidia said Huang would remain CEO during the review and had committed to cooperating.
Amy Kremer, chairwoman of advocacy group Humans First, said Huang should resign and called for federal investigations.
"He is compromised," Kremer told Fox News Digital. "We have to get to the bottom of this and let’s hope that he’s the only one."

Kremer also called for Nvidia to lose government contracts until Huang leaves the company. She criticized his advocacy for easing restrictions on chip sales to China, arguing the reported relationship raises national security concerns.
The allegations have not established that Huang knowingly shared information or that Nvidia’s technology was compromised.

President Donald Trump said he spoke with Huang Monday and believes the Nvidia CEO "will be in good shape," while adding that he did not expect to raise the allegations with Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Reuters/Evan Vucci)
Trump said Monday he spoke with Huang and believed the Nvidia CEO "will be in good shape," while expressing amazement at the allegations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump also said he did not think he would raise the matter with Xi.
The White House declined to elaborate on whether the Trump administration would continue engaging with Huang, referring Fox News Digital to Trump’s previous comments.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump signals surprising approach to choosing his successor as GOP's 2028 field grows
summary: Trump says he may not endorse in the 2028 Republican Party presidential primary
story: Vance or Rubio? MAGA voters speaking with Fox News Digital ahead of a recent Trump rally reveal their early picks for 2028 Republican presidential nomination
President Donald Trump says he may not put his thumb on the scale when it comes to picking the Republican Party's 2028 presidential nominee.

"Probably, not necessarily," Trump said in a post-midterm election interview on CBS' "60 Minutes" when asked whether he will endorse in the primary to pick the next Republican nominee. "So I may or may not get involved... Maybe I'm better off not getting involved."
Trump for months has touted the GOP's "great bench" when asked about the likely Republican field of contenders aiming to succeed him in the White House.
The president reiterated that opinion after the GOP's drubbing in last week's midterm elections, as the party lost control of both the House and the Senate.
VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS
President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)

"I think we have an unbelievable bench of talent," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum in an election night interview on Fox News.. "We have a great group of talented people that I think would do a very good job."

Early jockeying by the potential contenders began the morning after Election Day, with midterm post-mortems by Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis grabbing plenty of headlines.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"There's going to be a robust field of candidates that test the waters in Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina and that's exactly as it should be," Nicole Schlinger, a veteran Iowa-based Republican strategist, told Fox News Digital. "We're going to get an opportunity to see which approach to our message of where we as the Republican Party goes next is going to resonate the most with the grassroots voters who are going to show up and kick tires."

Here's a look at the list of potential GOP presidential contenders in the burgeoning race to become the party's next standard-bearer and impact which direction the party will head in a post-Trump era.
Vice President JD Vance
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport, Nov. 2, 2026, in Rome, N.Y. (Tom Brenner/Pool Photo via AP)
The vice president has long been viewed as the likely frontrunner for the 2028 GOP nomination and Trump's heir apparent.

But the conventional wisdom from pundits is that the shellacking the GOP took in the midterms has transformed what may have been a Vance coronation into a more competitive and crowded nomination battle.

Vance kicked off the post-midterms debate last Wednesday morning with a roughly 600-word postmortem on X, blaming the war with Iran for the ballot box setbacks, in what some pundits viewed as an early pitch to eventually claim the MAGA and America First mantle.

Even with last week's setbacks, Vance leads many of the early 2028 GOP presidential primary polls, has built a formidable fundraising network thanks in part to his role as the Republican National Committee's finance chair, and has a team of advisors and aides that would form the beginnings of a presidential campaign.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio
Secretary of State Marco Rubio attends a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 7. (Yves Herman/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Rubio, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination, is doing his best to stay far away from the 2028 spotlight.

The former senator from Florida has long been floated by Trump and by pundits as a possible White House contender, and his support in early 2028 polls has soared. But Rubio has downplayed such speculation, and dismissed reports he was considering stepping down as secretary of state to lay the groundwork for a presidential run.

Rubio, who has said a handful of times over the past year that he'd back Vance if the vice president decides to launch a White House campaign, was asked about 2028 Monday while taking questions from reporters during a stop in France.
"I don't know why you're wasting your time," Rubio said. "I'm not going to talk about 2028 any longer. I'm just not going to talk about 2028 anymore."
Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks during a campaign rally with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Grosse Point Woods, Mich., Oct. 28, 2026. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)
The conservative firebrand senator from Texas, who was runner-up to Trump in the bruising 2016 presidential primaries, has made no secret that he may run for the White House again in 2028.
In his post-Election Day assessment, Cruz described the midterms as a "blue tsunami" and warned that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State.
"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."
In a possible preview of the Republican primaries, Cruz has put plenty of daylight between himself and Vance over support for Israel, with Cruz spotlighting his support for the Israeli government.
Boosting Cruz if he decides to run would be his top-ranked podcast, "Verdict with Ted Cruz," which has allowed the senator to build a massive grassroots network.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis
Gov. Ron DeSantis holds a press conference at the State Emergency Operations Center regarding Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 8, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters)

The term-limited conservative Florida governor, who finishes up in Tallahassee at the start of the new year, ran for the White House in 2024. He was an early frontrunner before being decisively defeated by Trump.
DeSantis held a news conference the morning after Election Day when he called the midterm election results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country."

"Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt — not just for the next two years... That is something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he said. "We knew it could be worse. I don't think most of us thought it would be this bad."

But DeSantis, who sat for a slew of media interviews in the wake of the midterms, repeatedly highlighted that "the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida."

While 2028 buzz about DeSantis surged since last week's election, the governor took to social media on Friday to blast a report that he was planning a 2028 run, emphasizing, "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything. Just another pathetic attempt to garner clicks."
Former Vice President Mike Pence
Former Vice President Mike Pence is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on March 18, 2026, in Washington D.C. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Pence, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, has said he has "no plans" to run for the White House again in 2028.
But Pence has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year.

And Trump's first vice president told Fox News Digital earlier this year that his fight to keep the Republican Party from drifting too far from its conservative roots and principles, amid a rise of populism in the GOP and big government creep during Trump's second administration, is "the calling of my life right now."

Last week Pence argued, "The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism, and our majorities in Congress and state legislatures and governorships across the country paid the price."
But he emphasized, "The conservative comeback starts today."
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp
Term-limited GOP Gov. Brian Kemp, right, endorses Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the Republican gubernatorial runoff, in Atlanta, Georgia, on June 15, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
The conservative term-limited governor, who finishes out his tenure in Atlanta in two months, is also seen as a potential White House contender.
In the wake of the midterm shellacking, Kemp spelled out a GOP vision centered on the "conservative principles of our party."
"It’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come," the governor wrote.
Former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin

Former GOP Gov. Glenn Youngkin of Virginia, left, teams up on the campaign trail on the eve of the Wisconsin primary with Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, on Aug. 10, 2026, in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Youngkin, who instantly soared to political stardom after his 2021 gubernatorial victory energized Republicans a year after Trump lost the White House and the Senate in the 2020 election, has consistently downplayed talk of a 2028 presidential campaign.
Instead, Youngkin has focused on his signature issue  — education  — by pushing to promote school choice programs through his recently formed national policy group Empowering America's Parents.
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, a 2024 Republican presidential candidate, is interviewed on the campaign trail by Fox News Digital. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Christie, who unsuccessfully ran for the 2016 and 2024 GOP nominations, is seriously mulling a third run for the White House.

"The midterms were a repudiation of the GOP and Donald Trump. It is time Republicans do the autopsy, learn the lessons and move forward," Christie, a vocal Republican critic of the president, argued in the days after last week's election. "The Trump era is over. He has led us to the greatest losses this country has seen for a party since Richard Nixon."
Christie has said he'll decide on a presidential run in the next few months, telling Fox News Digital recently, "I think there’s a lot of flexibility on the timing."
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., arrives at a House Republican Conference meeting in the U.S. Capitol Building on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Bacon, a former Air Force brigadier general who has at times split with Trump on foreign policy and national security issues, decided against running for re-election this year and exits Congress in two months.
Bacon has said he is open to a potential run for president in 2028 or serving in a supporting role on another Republican candidate's ticket.
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders participates in the first National Outdoor Recreation Executive Forum on May 7, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Outdoor Recreation Roundtable)
Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as Trump’s White House press secretary for much of his first term.
Sanders, who made history four years ago as the first woman elected Arkansas governor and last week won re-election by double digits, is increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender.
Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas

Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas joins GOP colleagues in speaking to reporters following Senate Republican policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 23, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Cotton, who took a hard look at a 2024 GOP presidential run before deciding against launching a campaign, was just re-elected.

The senator, an Army veteran who served in combat in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars before becoming a rising star in the Republican Party and who was on Trump's running mate short list two years ago, is also viewed as a potential White House hopeful.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida
Republican Sen. Rick Scott is interviewed by Fox News Digital on March 6, 2026, in Palm Beach, Florida. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Scott, a self-made multimillionaire and former two-term governor who's the wealthiest member of the Senate, also mulled a 2024 bid before running for re-election.

Midterm election campaign trail stops in Iowa and New Hampshire  — the two states that lead off the Republican presidential nominating calendar  — sparked speculation that Scott was considering a 2028 campaign.
Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., speaks to members of the media at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kennedy, who's up for re-election in 2028, has said he would consider a White House run instead of seeking another term in the Senate if he felt he could no longer be effective in the Senate or if he felt dissatisfied with the Republican presidential primary field.
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo (Siavosh Hosseini/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Pompeo, a former four-term congressman from Kansas who served as CIA director and later as the top U.S. diplomat in Trump's first administration, also took a hard look at a 2024 run before passing.
Asked last year about a 2028 bid, Pompeo told Fox News Digital, "We'll see what the good Lord brings in a couple of years."
He's currently viewed by pundits as a possible contender.
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on May 18, 2026, in Mason County, Kentucky (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

The vocal Republican critic of the president who relentlessly pressed for the release of the Epstein files before losing his bid for renomination earlier this year to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein has said he's "not ruling anything in or out" when it comes to a presidential bid.

Last week, Axios first reported that a group of Libertarian Party operatives and anti-Trump MAGA defectors was urging Massie to run for the White House as a third-party or Libertarian presidential candidate.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Dem governor’s tale of combat action torn to shreds by commanding Army officer: 'Give me a break'
summary: Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore's former Army supervisor in Afghanistan says his claims of leading paratroopers in combat are "not truthful."
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Retired Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling who pushed back against Moore’s claims that he "led paratroopers in combat" in Afghanistan.

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, widely believed to be considering a presidential run in 2028, is facing renewed scrutiny over his resume — this time from his former Army supervisor who is questioning the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat.

In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, The Baltimore Sun spoke with a retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas.
Moore's team said that "partisan politics got in the way" and led to Gottschling's latest assessment, where he told Fox News Digital: "I wouldn't call him a soldier."
Fox News Digital spoke with Gottschling on Monday.

Maryland Governor Wes Moore speaks onstage during the 2025 ESSENCE Festival Of Culture presented by Coca-Cola - Day 3 at Ernest N. Morial Convention Center on July 6, 2025, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for ESSENCE)
WES MOORE PREEMPTIVELY UNLOADS ON BALTIMORE SUN AHEAD OF EXPOSE, AS SPOX BEEFS WITH 'RIGHT WING' OWNERSHIP

He said in the interview that while Moore would occasionally leave the base, the governor never saw combat. Gottschling said he would describe Moore and himself as "combat veterans" who are "not veterans of combat."

"When you think of a veteran of combat, you think somebody that's in a foxhole, getting shot at, IED blowing up the convoy, or even more dramatically, when you think about World War II movies, Easy Company, or any of those things where it's like, those guys are getting shot," Gottschling said. "That just wasn't the environment that he was in."

"He starts talking about, you know, in his TED Talk and really struggling with reintegration into the civilian world after the deployment, I'm like, 'what is he talking about?' You know, he spent six months over there, basically in, you know, a forward base that pretty much is as safe as anywhere. You'd probably be at more risk going to an ER in any of the cities in the United States than you would be in Afghanistan, in Salerno."

Sgt. Matthew Taylor from Orlando, Florida, 1st Lt. Wes Brockbank from Seattle, Washington, and CPL Matthew Moebes from Decatur, Alabama with the U.S. Army's 4th Squadron 2nd Cavalry Regiment walk through a village during a joint patrol with Afghan National Army soldiers near Kandahar, Afghanistan, on March 2, 2014. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Moore is widely considered a contender for the 2028 Democratic Party nominee for president.

"I just think it's disingenuous to really associate with the struggle. I mean you can have some empathy for people that might struggle with the transition, but when you come over there pretty much dip into a combat zone situation, work on the staff for six months and then come out you know saying that, you know, all this trauma that you had ... and it's like, oh, give me a break," Gottschling told Fox News Digital.
"So I think it's just him emotionalizing and capitalizing on what soldiers do. And he's not a soldier," he continued.
"He was in the Army as a reservist in a staff position in Iraq, but I wouldn't call him a soldier."

The Baltimore Sun report describes Gottschling, who then held the rank of major, as the "Army officer who supervised Moore daily" in Afghanistan. Moore has framed himself as a paratrooper in the famed 82nd Airborne Division who led troops into battle during his deployment overseas.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore speaks during a press conference at the Maryland State House on August 5, 2025, in Annapolis, Maryland. (Jamie Sabau/Getty Images)

Moore worked on information operations coordination while the pair were stationed together at Forward Operating Base Salerno in the Khost Province near Afghanistan's border with Pakistan. According to The Baltimore Sun, Moore's job was "analyzing reports from infantry battalions and provincial reconstruction teams, coordinating for civilian assistance and helping Afghan officials communicate with the public."
Central to Moore's personal narrative is that he led troops into combat in Afghanistan. He said that on multiple occasions on X while he was campaigning for Maryland's governorship.
WES MOORE WARNS DHS FEDERAL OCCUPATION OF NEW ICE COMPOUND NOW UNDER STATE INVESTIGATION
"I’ve seen real patriotism when I led paratroopers in combat in Afghanistan and I’ve seen it in my own family," he said in a Nov. 6, 2022 post, just two days before he was elected governor.
"Service has defined my life, starting when I joined the Army when I was 17, through leading soldiers in combat with the 82nd Airborne in Afghanistan, to today," he said in a post earlier that year.
In his book, "The Work," Moore describes being shot at.

"As a soldier, you never forget the first time you were shot at," he wrote in the book. "A sudden, stunning commotion engulfs you—the sound of shells buzzing past your ears, a flurry of divots leaping out of the earth around your feet—but then your training kicks in," the book says.
"Moments before those first shots came at me, I was convinced I was prepared for the experience," the book continues.
MARYLAND'S LONE CONGRESSIONAL REPUBLICAN BLASTS MOORE'S REDISTRICTING PUSH AS ALLEGED 2028 WHITE HOUSE PLAY

Moore, who is widely considered a contender for the Democratic nominee for president in 2028, reaffirmed that that passage from his book was true during a July interview with CNN, again claiming that he "led soldiers in combat."

Gottschling also contests the extent to which Moore led other soldiers. In "The Work," Moore described fellow soldiers as "my paratroopers" and rejects Moore's framing that he was ever "leading" troops in combat.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moore's senior press secretary described Gottschling's motives as political.

"Five days after Marylanders re-elected Governor Moore in a historic landslide, Sinclair is back to swiftboating a veteran by recycling the exact same stories and interviews they already ran months ago," Ammar Moussa said. "Twenty years ago, before partisan politics got in the way, Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling signed an official Army evaluation declaring Wes Moore a ‘top 1% officer’ and ‘the best lieutenant I've encountered during Operation Enduring Freedom.'"

U.S. service members walk off a helicopter on the runway at Camp Bost in Helmand Province, Afghanistan, on Sept. 11, 2017. About 300 Marines are deployed in Helmand Province in a train, advise and assist role supporting local Afghan security forces. (Andrew Renneisen/Getty Images)
Gottschling addressed that evaluation with The Baltimore Sun.

"There’s a lot of embellishment with that, but that’s just how the system was," he told the outlet. "You’re not trying to be deceitful about it, but you want to elevate what they did (your soldiers) … so they can get their next job or next promotion."

"Now, a longtime Donald Trump donor who has openly stated his goal is to stop Governor Moore from being in contention for the presidency is working with Sinclair to contradict his own signed military records," Moussa continued. "Governor Moore’s service in Afghanistan—including earning the Combat Action Badge and coming under rocket fire alongside fellow service members—has been independently verified by official Army records and The Baltimore Banner, which interviewed fellow service members, and no partisan swiftboat campaign will change the facts."
The Combat Action Badge is also addressed in The Baltimore Sun's story. The story describes it as a "minor indirect rocket attack" where nobody was injured.

Chelsea Clinton and Gov. Wes Moore speak onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative)
Moussa, citing a report in the Baltimore Banner, said a Marine named Anthony Del Signore who was attached to Moore's unit said that their convoy "took some shots" at least once.

A New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one.
In a story published in July on the topic of Moore's military service, Gottschling said he doesn't want Moore to be president. At that time, Moore was running for reelection as governor.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I care about my faith and country. I do not really care whether Moore is elected governor of Maryland, but I do care if he is in contention for the presidency," he said. "I could not live with myself if I was not vocal about the truth."

Gottschling made it clear that he wasn't putting down Moore's service, which he called exemplary, but took issue with what Moore said about his service after he came home and elevated his political profile.
Gottschling called Moore a "valued staff officer" and said he "appreciated every minute" of the work he did.

"I think there's nothing wrong with that, if it ended there, that would be it," Gottschling said. "But it didn't end there. The embellishment, the aggrandizing of his actions over there that didn't take place is the problem that I have. I'm a pursuer of the truth, you know, and I want to tell the truth."
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: GOP wipeout goes from bad to worse as Dems quietly score another major win with big ramifications
summary: Democrats flipped legislative chambers in Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona and other battleground states, creating trifectas that could reshape redistricting.
story: Midterm election results prompt intense scrutiny as host Liz Claman analyzes voter concern over rising inflation and the cost of living. Fox News contributors Joe Concha and Jessica Tarlov join the discussion to break down how a 79% hardship rating on inflation impacted GOP candidates. The panel examines the economic message heading into future political contests.

In addition to taking control of the House of Representatives, the Senate, and the majority of governorships on Tuesday, Democrats have also assumed control of the majority of state legislatures across the country for the first time in over a decade.

Heading into the election, Republicans controlled 28 of the nation’s 49 bicameral state legislatures, compared with 18 controlled by Democrats, while three states had divided control. Democrats now control both chambers in 24 states, compared with 22 for Republicans. North Carolina and Texas have split legislatures, while races in Alaska and Georgia remain pending. Even if Republicans win the uncalled chambers in the pending states, Democrats will still control more state legislatures than Republicans.
Nebraska is included in the Republican count because its officially nonpartisan, unicameral legislature is led by a Republican majority.

Democrats scored major victories in several pivotal battleground states during the 2026 midterms, flipping legislative chambers and securing full control of state governments in places that will shape redistricting and election rules ahead of 2028. In Wisconsin, Democrats captured both the Assembly and Senate for the first time in years, pairing the wins with the governorship to create a trifecta.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Democrats seized control of the majority of state legislatures across the country on Tuesday night, in addition to taking control of Congress and the majority of governorships. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images ; Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)

Similar gains unfolded in Michigan, where the party flipped the House and expanded its Senate majority alongside a Democratic governor, and in Minnesota, where Democrats reclaimed the House, held the Senate, and won the governorship. Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the Senate while retaining the House, and Arizona voters handed Democrats majorities in both chambers. New Hampshire also saw Democrats flip both houses of the legislature, while the party picked up the House in Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas.

The shift gives Democrats significantly more power to shape policy across the country as state lawmakers play a central role in setting election rules, drawing congressional maps, approving budgets and advancing laws on issues ranging from abortion and guns to education and labor.

The change could also have major implications for redistricting. States will redraw congressional and legislative maps after the 2030 census, and the party controlling state government will have greater influence over how those districts are designed. Democratic control could also lead to legal battles over existing maps and efforts to alter election administration rules ahead of future presidential contests.
HOUSE DEM WHO DEFIED HAKEEM JEFFRIES SCORES UPSET WIN IN PRO-TRUMP DISTRICT
Breakdown of who holds power in state legislatures across the country after Tuesday's midterm elections. (Fox News)

Democrats could similarly revive efforts to pass stricter gun laws, increase funding for public education and expand labor protections. Depending on the state, lawmakers could also target voting restrictions, expand access to mail-in and early voting, or change how elections are administered.
Results confirming Democratic control of the majority of state legislatures come days after the party captured control of both chambers of Congress and the majority of governorships.
Axios reports that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The sun shines on the Minnesota State Capitol on Feb. 12, 2024, in St. Paul. (Steve Karnowski/Associated Press)

"In a historic victory, Democrats now hold more than half of the seats at the state legislative level nationwide," Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams said in a press release. "These victories reinforce the DLCC’s national strategy to build power for Democrats all across the country. Whether competing for new majorities, breaking GOP supermajorities, or gaining seats to give Democrats more leverage to fight for their constituents, when these races have the resources they need, we can deliver wins in red, blue, and purple states alike."
Additionally, Democrats may now have the necessary votes to move forward with the National Popular Vote plan, which would bypass the Electoral College, Fox News Digital reported on Sunday.
The economy, government corruption, war in Iran and increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump's job performance created a perfect storm for Democrats, Fox News voter polling showed.

Voters cast their ballots with a bleak view of the country in their minds. Three-quarters said they felt dissatisfied or angry about how things were going, while just a quarter were satisfied or enthusiastic.

Three-quarters rated the economy negatively, a stark reversal from this point in Trump’s first term, when positive ratings outnumbered negative ones by 2-to-1, as shown in the 2018 Fox News Voter Analysis survey (66% positive, 34% negative).
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Explosive House report exposes failures it says allowed Epstein's abuse to continue for years
summary: House Republicans uncovered alleged conflicts of interest involving federal prosecutors and failures by financial institutions that enabled Epstein's yearslong abuse.
story: Vice President JD Vance discusses criticism of President Donald Trump over his ties to Jeffrey Epstein on ‘Hannity.’

FIRST ON FOX: The House Oversight Committee released a report concluding that prosecutorial failures, preferential treatment and institutional negligence allowed Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell to continue sexually exploiting young women and girls for years.

The investigation, led by Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest involving federal prosecutors, financial institutions that overlooked warning signs of sex trafficking and individuals accused of facilitating Epstein's abuse.
The report identified two former federal prosecutors whose involvement in Epstein's original investigation raised potential conflicts of interest.

Matthew Menchel, a senior federal prosecutor who recommended resolving Epstein's case through a non-prosecution agreement, previously had a romantic relationship with Lilly Ann Sanchez, who later represented Epstein.
Menchel did not recuse himself from the investigation and continued communicating and meeting with Epstein after the agreement, according to documents cited by the committee.

The House Oversight Committee report concludes prosecutorial failures and preferential treatment allowed Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell to exploit victims for years. (Joe Schildhorn/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS

Investigators also learned of an alleged photograph showing Menchel skiing with Epstein in Colorado in the early 2000s but could not verify its existence or establish that Menchel's decisions were improperly influenced.

Menchel, however, denied ever having skied with Epstein in a statement to the Miami Herald but did not deny meeting with him after leaving the U.S. Attorney's Office. His attorneys said their correspondence concerned potential legal representation and referrals, none of which resulted in business.

His attorneys also maintained that Menchel was not responsible for the final plea agreement, which was more lenient than the arrangement he recommended. A 2020 Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility report found that Menchel failed to disclose his relationship with Sanchez to supervisors but found no evidence of prosecutorial misconduct.
Sanchez did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Former federal prosecutor Bruce Reinhart established a private law practice while employed by the U.S. Attorney's Office and later represented Epstein associates. His practice was involved in matters related to Epstein's work-release program.
Former U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta testified that he did not know whether Reinhart had access to information about the Epstein investigation.
Reinhart did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The committee said it urged the Justice Department to investigate further former Miami Beach Mayor Philip Levine and celebrity hairstylist Frédéric Fekkai further, following testimony from Sarah Kellen, a former Epstein assistant who alleged that Epstein and the two associates sexually abused her.
Both Levine and Fekkai have denied the allegations in earlier statements. Levine and Fekkai did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Kellen also testified that Epstein instructed another assistant to remove computers, hard drives and other equipment from his Palm Beach residence before authorities searched the property in 2005. Investigators believed the equipment could contain evidence of sexual exploitation.

Epstein's attorney, Darren Indyke, testified that he later learned the hard drives were in the possession of private investigators. Federal investigators identified a potential lead concerning the equipment but abandoned the effort before finalizing Epstein's non-prosecution agreement.

The report also examined whether Sandy Berger, former national security advisor to President Bill Clinton, warned Epstein about the search, given that he sent Epstein an urgent message 18 days before the search. However, the committee found no evidence establishing that Berger tipped him off or that the message concerned the investigation.
House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., speaks at a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 21, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)
CLINTON JUDGE ORDERS DOJ TO UNSEAL THE EPSTEIN FILES IT HAS BEEN KEEPING HIDDEN
The committee recommended further investigations, stronger protections for trafficking survivors and reforms to prevent similar federal law enforcement failures.
Among those recommended for further investigation was Lesley Groff, Epstein's executive assistant for nearly two decades.

Groff, who scheduled Epstein's daily massage appointments and coordinated travel and lodging for women visiting his properties, testified that she was unaware he was sexually abusing young women and girls.
Groff continued working for Epstein after his 2008 conviction.
Groff did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
The committee also criticized Epstein's treatment following his 2008 conviction, arguing that his work-release privileges allowed him to continue abusing women.
Epstein served approximately 13 months of an 18-month sentence and was permitted to leave jail for up to 12 hours daily, six days a week.

His privileges included working at the Florida Science Foundation, which the committee described as a sham organization, traveling in private vehicles accompanied by paid off-duty sheriff's deputies, meeting visitors without continuous monitoring and visiting his Palm Beach residence.
Kellen and other survivors alleged that Epstein continued sexually abusing them during his work release.

The investigation also examined Epstein's relationships with prominent politicians, business executives and academic institutions, including billionaire Bill Gates and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Lutnick told the Oversight Committee in 2026 that he had "done absolutely nothing wrong." He acknowledged visiting Epstein's private island for lunch with his family in 2012, despite previously claiming he had cut ties with Epstein in 2005. Lutnick said he could not recall why his family had lunch there. Comer said Lutnick addressed the discrepancy in his opening statement.

Gates testified that Epstein requested reimbursement for expenses involving a woman with whom Gates had an affair. Gates said he refused to pay, ended his relationship with Epstein in late 2014 and was never a client of Epstein's financial businesses.
Gates and Lutnick did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates attends a dinner hosted by President Donald Trump with technology leaders in the State Dining Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., Sept. 4, 2025. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
The committee also identified billionaire financier Leon Black as a major source of Epstein's income following his 2008 conviction.
Black paid Epstein approximately $158 million to $170 million for purported tax and estate planning services.

The committee identified an agreement involving a woman with whom Black had an extramarital relationship that reportedly required payments of $100,000 per month for 15 years, among other benefits, in exchange for confidentiality. Epstein reportedly advised Black on the agreement.
Black cited an independent investigation that found he was not involved in Epstein's criminal activities, although the committee questioned its independence.
EPSTEIN-LINKED BILLIONAIRE POURS $500K INTO SUPER PAC BACKING KENTUCKY DEMOCRAT: 'DIRTY EPSTEIN-CLASS MONEY'
Black also refused to fully answer certain committee questions and failed to comply with subpoenas, prompting a unanimous House vote in September 2026 to hold him in criminal contempt of Congress.
Black did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
The report also examined Epstein's relationships with current and former public officials.

Kathryn Ruemmler, former White House counsel under President Barack Obama, maintained a professional relationship with Epstein after his 2008 conviction and received expensive gifts, including designer handbags, boots, spa services and travel upgrades.
A close-up of Jeffrey Epstein. (Rick Friedman/Rick Friedman Photography/Corbis via Getty Images)
In a 2016 email, Ruemmler joked about receiving the "best massage ever but not your kind of massage."
Ruemmler acknowledged that the remark was in poor taste and testified that she believed Epstein had resolved his criminal case and was living lawfully.
She also testified that a May 2019 meeting with Epstein concerned potential litigation threatened by attorney Michael Avenatti, not a criminal investigation.
The report identified Del. Stacey Plaskett, D-V.I., as having exchanged text messages with Epstein during a 2019 congressional hearing, including communications about questioning a witness.

Plaskett did not deny exchanging the messages. Her office said she received texts from staff, constituents and members of the public, including Epstein, whom she described as a constituent who contacted her following a widely circulated hearing exchange. The committee did not allege wrongdoing by Plaskett.
Ruemmler and Plaskett did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
The report also cited an email indicating that House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries' campaign solicited a donation from Epstein.

Jeffries, however, said he had no recollection of the email and had never met or communicated with Epstein. Federal election records reportedly show no donations from Epstein to Jeffries or the committees involved. Reports identified Lisa Rossi of the political consulting firm Dynamic SRG as the sender of the message.
Jeffries did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
EXCLUSIVE: OSSOFF CHALLENGED TO RETURN EPSTEIN-LINKED DONATION OR RETRACT ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK
House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer subpoenaed Jeffrey Epstein's estate in a continuation of his panel's probe. (Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Regarding Epstein's death in 2019, the committee identified serious prison security failures but did not overturn the official suicide finding.
The report also criticized the Justice Department for missing disclosure deadlines and exposing survivors' personal information during the release of millions of Epstein-related documents.

The Republican-led investigation stated that it uncovered no evidence implicating President Donald Trump in Epstein's criminal activities and accused congressional Democrats of politicizing the investigation.

title: GOP lawmaker ousts fellow Republican in gerrymandered California district
summary: Republican Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a rare GOP vs. GOP battle forced by California Gov. Gavin Newsom's redistricting in the midterms.
story: Outgoing Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., says the GOP House delegation from his state is dropping to four or fewer seats out of 52 — less than 10% — despite 40-45% of the state’s voters being Republican, calling it pure gerrymandering.
Gov. Gavin Newsom-signed California redistricting has scored at least a 2-for-1 consolidation of House Republicans.

Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., is projected to defeat fellow Rep. Young Kim, R-Calif., in the 40th Congressional District race called Monday night, ostensibly forcing two incumbents to battle for one seat in the gerrymandered district.

"I want to congratulate Congressman Ken Calvert on his victory," Kim wrote in a statement posted to X, sharply criticizing the map that effectively drew one of them out. "I wish him the very best as he continues representing our communities. It is unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members of Congress into this race."
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

California Republican Reps. Ken Calvert and Young Kim were forced to run against each other in the newly redrawn 40th Congressional District. Now the California House GOP is cut in more than half. (Getty Images)

All told, Democrats' redistricting and the so-called blue wave have more than cut the Republican California delegation in half, from nine seats (eight Republicans and one independent that caucuses with them) to just three or four (one race remains too close to call a week after the election).
Calvert, the longest-serving Republican in California’s House delegation, had declared victory days earlier while ballots were still being counted.
The district covers suburban communities in eastern Orange County and stretches into the Inland Empire in western Riverside County — southeast of Los Angeles.

California voters approved the Democratic-backed redistricting plan that combined portions of the two lawmakers' previous districts into a single seat, setting up the rare intraparty contest in one of the state’s remaining Republican strongholds. Kim had represented the area since 2018. Calvert's prior district, which included much of Riverside County and Palm Springs, was carved up and redistributed.
ALL THE REPUBLICAN HOUSE MEMBERS OUSTED FROM CONGRESS

Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., is the longest-standing House Republican from the state, which had what was once nine seats whittled to at most four with one race still too close to call. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Calvert is just one of three House Republicans in the state to survive thus far.

Rep. Tom McClintock, R-Calif., and Rep. Vince Fong, R-Calif., won re-election in the 5th and 20th Congressional Districts. Those are heavily Republican stretches of the Central Valley and Sierra Nevada foothills — rural agricultural and mountain country well inland, roughly between San Francisco and Los Angeles but far from both coastal metros in the western parts of the state.

Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., is clinging to a narrow lead of just 3,384 votes over Democratic challenger Tessa Lynn Hodge in California's 23rd Congressional District, a High Desert seat in San Bernardino County that was rated Solid R by the Fox News Power Rankings before the midterms.
With ballots still being counted, Obernolte holds just a 1.6-point edge — about 50.8% to 49.2% — after winning the district by more than 20 points in 2024.
BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS
Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., listens in as Rep. David Valadao, R-Calif., speaks to the media at a campaign event in September before his November loss. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)
Four other Republicans from California are leaving Congress in January 2027.
Rep. James Gallagher, R-Calif., lost to Democrat Mike McGuire by nearly 13 points, while Rep. David Valadao, R-Calif., lost to Democrat Randy Villegas by nearly 37 points.
Rep. Kevin Kiley, I-Calif., who left the Republican Party to try to keep his seat as an independent, lost by more than 17 points to Democrat Richard Pan.
Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., did not seek re-election and his former seat flipped to blue under the new map, with Democrat Marni von Wilpert defeating Republican Jim Desmond by nearly 20 points.
CALIFORNIA VOTERS DECIDE WHO WILL SUCCEED NEWSOM IN CONSEQUENTIAL GOVERNOR'S RACE

Rep. James Gallagher, R-Calif., was among the Republicans from the state to not survive this midterm blue wave that reduced the red in California by half. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
He ripped the "gerrymander" effort by Democrats in making California look even deeper blue than it already is.

"There are currently no more than four out of what was eight," he told reporters Tuesday morning on Capitol Hill. "If it remains where it is today, then there'll be four or less than 10% of the 52 members.

"It's a big change, but it's the result of gerrymandering," he continued. "About 40-45% of the voters in California are Republicans, in presidential races and so on. So you really have called it a 60-40 relationship, and then you have only 10 – less than 10% – so that's what gerrymandering does: It distorts what would otherwise be – not even – but a relatively similar amount of members."
Calvert against Kim was the lone GOP vs. GOP battle left by the new map.

"As an immigrant who came to the United States in pursuit of the American Dream, serving this nation in Congress has been one of the greatest honors of my life," Kim wrote in her statement posted to X late Monday night. "It has been a privilege to give back to the community that has given me so much, and I am incredibly grateful to my family, our volunteers, supporters, and everyone who placed their trust in me throughout this campaign."
DEM WINS TRUMP-TARGETED TEXAS DISTRICT IN REBUKE OF REPUBLICAN REDISTRICTING SHAKEUP

Kim said she was proud of the record built "delivering results for our communities, working to secure our country at home and abroad, strengthen our economy, and make life safer and more affordable for California families."
During the campaign, both candidates supported President Donald Trump’s agenda early on and later sought to project themselves as pragmatic conservatives.
The race turned negative, with Kim citing ethics complaints and an FBI investigation into some of Calvert’s real estate dealings. Calvert denied the allegations and was never charged.

Calvert highlighted a campaign donation Kim received from a Chinese American businessman who has faced scrutiny over alleged foreign influence. Kim returned the contribution and said she was unaware of the claims.

"With the passage of Prop 50, Californians were sold a bill of goods, allowing Gavin Newsom and his radical allies in Sacramento an unprecedented power grab to redraw the Congressional map and silence those who disagree with his extreme policies," Calvert wrote on X a year ago.
"Gerrymandering districts because you don’t like the results of an election is politics at its absolute worst.

"Governor Newsom pouring millions into this ballot initiative while crime goes unchecked, housing costs skyrocket, and taxes as well as gas prices remain among the highest in the nation shows he’s more interested in protecting his party’s stranglehold on the state than delivering on the issues families face. Despite the passage of Prop 50, I am determined to keep fighting for the families I represent in Congress."

title: Hegseth rips impeachment push from outgoing Republican as 'farce,' 'stunt'
summary: War Secretary Pete Hegseth, facing a House impeachment effort, delivers remarks at the first Pengton news conference since May, having focused on the Iran conflict and CENTCOM Strait of Hormuz blockade.
story: Sec. of War Pete Hegseth denounces Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment effort as a political stunt during his opening remarks at a Pentagon press conference.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth, facing eight articles of impeachment in a privileged House resolution, remains defiant amid kinetic war and political warfare.
Hegseth said he stood behind military operations in Iran, Venezuela and Yemen, describing them as lawful.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said in a Tuesday morning conference. "Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president, this country and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it."
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it."
TRUMP DEFENDS PENTAGON CHIEF AS MASSIE TARGETS HIM: 'HEGSETH SHOULD BE PRAISED, NOT IMPEACHED'
President Donald Trump gave a real-time review of Hegseth's remarks in a post Tuesday morning on Truth Social.
"Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" Trump wrote.

"We destroyed terror regimes' capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it's the job well done."
"I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow," he added.
TRUMP GIVES HEGSETH AN ‘A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS’ FOR REJECTION OF WEAPONIZED IMPEACHMENT
Hegseth said the impeachment effort hands U.S. enemies a "propaganda victory."

"This is not patriotism; this is sabotage. It tells our enemies that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations," Hegseth added.
Impeachment has been one-sided against Trump, he noted, saying past presidents have been immune amid war efforts.

"No secretary of war or secretary of defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations and, in our case, successful ones at that," Hegseth said. "Not once – war powers resolution or not."

"Not under Reagan in Lebanon, not under Clinton in Kosovo, not under Obama in Iraq and Syria, not under Biden in Iraq and Syria. That's the standard. The history is clear, and it's very straightforward. And one disgruntled congressman wants to shred it over policy disagreements."
HEGSETH'S FUTURE DRAWS OMINOUS PREDICTIONS FROM INSIDERS AFTER GOP LOSSES, BUT TRUMP ISN'T BUDGING YET

"That's what it is: Policy disagreements," he continued. "Not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.

"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement: It's legislation; it's debate; it's the next presidential election. It's not handing the House and Senate floor to the Democrats so that they can run a show trial against the president and the secretary of war."
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH
Asked about Vance blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war, Hegseth said he agreed with the war.
"It was done for the right reasons to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon," the war secretary said.
Speaking at a G7 summit in France, Secretary of State Marco Rubio weighed in on the impeachment effort.

"The president of United States is the commander in chief, and he has a right to defend this country and to address imminent threats that pose a threat to the United States – and he's done so," Rubio told a Paris press gaggle minutes after the Hegseth news conference. "I don't know how anyone could argue that drug dealers trying to import poison into our country is not an imminent threat. It's a real and imminent threat, and it's been addressed."
Trump defended Hegseth against Massie's impeachment effort in a Truth Social post Monday night, too, saying his war secretary "should be praised, not impeached."

"With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" he added.

title: Is AI deciding who's dangerous in Michigan prisons?
summary: Michigan's new prison scoring system claims 30% better violence prediction, but Recidiviz says it doesn't actually use AI to classify inmates.
story: Incarcerated men participate in employment counseling at a Michigan prison, where security classifications can affect access to job training and educational opportunities. (Michigan Department of Corrections)

What if a computer-generated score could influence whether someone lives in a low-security prison dorm or a tightly controlled cell? Michigan is preparing to test new technology that could affect exactly that.

State officials say the system could improve predictions of future prison violence by approximately 30%. That's a big claim, especially when the safety of correctional officers and incarcerated people could depend on getting those assessments right.

But there's something important missing from early reports about Michigan prison AI. Despite headlines suggesting artificial intelligence will determine how dangerous someone might be, the nonprofit developing the software says AI plays no role in calculating security scores.

Instead, the technology follows predetermined rules, and corrections staff make the final decisions. So, how does the system work? And can Michigan really predict prison violence more accurately without putting too much trust in a computer-generated score?
FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH
